interview.question: What can `cy.get()` retrieve?
interview.answer: It accepts a CSS selector or an alias such as `@button`. A selector yields matching DOM elements; an alias can yield DOM elements, values, intercepts, spies, or stubs.
interview.followUp: How does an aliased DOM query behave after rerendering? By default, Cypress reruns the queries that created the alias, so it can reflect the current page. A static alias keeps the value captured when it was created.

interview.question: How does retrying and timeout behavior work?
interview.answer: `cy.get()` retries while looking for elements and also retries until chained assertions pass. It stops when the command timeout is reached, using `defaultCommandTimeout` unless a `timeout` option is supplied.
interview.followUp: How would you wait longer for a slow result? Pass a command option such as `{ timeout: 10000 }` or change `defaultCommandTimeout` globally.

interview.question: How does `cy.get()` differ from `.find()`?
interview.answer: Normally, `cy.get()` starts at the document. Inside `.within()`, it searches within the `.within()` subject. `.find()` differs because it always starts from the current subject.
interview.followUp: Which command should you use for a descendant query after selecting a container? Use `.find()` when the query must remain limited to that container's element tree.

keyPoints: Use a CSS selector to retrieve one or more matching DOM elements, or use an alias beginning with `@`.
A normal alias is live: Cypress repeats its original queries whenever the alias is requested.
Use a static alias when later commands must receive the earlier captured value instead of a fresh lookup.
The search normally begins at `cy.root`, which is usually the application document.
A comma-separated selector combines alternatives and returns elements matching any listed selector.
Prefer dedicated `data-*` attributes such as `data-cy` for selectors that are less affected by style or text changes.
Set `includeShadowDom: true` for one query, or configure shadow DOM traversal globally.
gotchas: `cy.get()` does not enter iframe documents. Use the documented iframe approach for same-origin iframe content.
Do not expect `cy.get()` to search inside the previous subject. Use `.find()` when the search must stay inside the current element.
For intercepted aliases, use `.1`, `.2`, and later indices. Use `.all` for every interception.

cy.getAllLocalStorage.explanation: Cypress reads localStorage for every origin that the test has used. It returns an object grouped by origin. When you chain a should assertion, Cypress reads storage again and retries the assertion until it passes or the command times out. A then callback runs only once after the read finishes.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options that change command behavior. log defaults to true and timeout defaults to defaultCommandTimeout.

cy.getAllLocalStorage.returns: An object keyed by origins. Each origin contains its localStorage key-value pairs.

example.title: Read localStorage for all origins
example.explanation: This visits a page, stores a value, and checks storage for that origin.

interview.question: What does cy.getAllLocalStorage() yield?
interview.answer: cy.getAllLocalStorage() returns an object whose keys are origins. Each origin maps to an object containing that origin's localStorage key-value pairs.
interview.followUp: What happens when storage is populated later? A directly chained should assertion causes Cypress to reread storage and retry until the assertion passes or the timeout is reached.

interview.question: How does this command retry?
interview.answer: It is a query. Cypress rereads localStorage from all used origins on each retry, and chained assertions control those retries.
interview.followUp: Does then provide the same behavior? No. then runs once after the command settles and receives one storage snapshot.

interview.question: Which options can be passed?
interview.answer: The command accepts an options object. log controls Command Log output, and timeout controls how long Cypress waits; timeout defaults to defaultCommandTimeout.
interview.followUp: How should a test change the wait limit? Pass a timeout value, such as cy.getAllLocalStorage({ timeout: 10000 }).should(...).

keyPoints: It reads localStorage for every origin that the test has used.
The result uses origins as keys, with each value holding that origin's stored items.
Directly chained assertions are retried until they pass or the command times out.
Each retry reads current storage again, so the result can reflect values added after the first read.
The log option controls whether the command appears in Cypress's Command Log.
The timeout option sets the waiting period before the command fails.
gotchas: Assertions inside then do not retry. Use a directly chained should assertion when storage may be written asynchronously.
Call this command from cy, not as a standalone function.
The command can time out while waiting for a chained assertion. You can set a timeout in the options object.

cy.getAllSessionStorage.returns: An object whose keys are origins and whose values are key-value pairs from sessionStorage.

interview.question: What does cy.getAllSessionStorage() return?
interview.answer: It reads sessionStorage for all origins that the test has interacted with. The result maps each origin to its stored key-value pairs.
interview.followUp: What happens when there is no storage data? The command yields an empty object until data exists, and a directly chained assertion can keep retrying.

interview.question: How does retry behavior work?

Call this command from cy, not as a standalone function.

interview.question: What does cy.getCookie() yield?
interview.answer: cy.getCookie() reads one browser cookie by name. It yields a cookie object when found and null when no matching cookie exists.
interview.followUp: How do you wait for a cookie set by an asynchronous login? Chain .should('exist') or another assertion, because assertions drive retries.

interview.question: How does the domain option affect cy.getCookie()?
interview.answer: The domain option selects the domain to read. Without it, Cypress uses the application under test hostname; before visiting a page, that can be the hostname serving the spec.
interview.followUp: Can it read a cookie from a sibling domain? Not directly through the current origin; use cy.origin() for the other origin or use cy.getAllCookies() when appropriate.

interview.question: Which properties can the yielded cookie object contain?

The command does not match cookies from a subdomain or sibling domain. Use the correct domain or run the command in cy.origin() for another origin.

interview.question: What does `cy.go()` do, and which arguments can it accept?
interview.answer: `cy.go()` navigates through the browser history. Use `back` or `forward` for one entry, or use a number such as `-1` or `1` for a relative history position.
interview.followUp: What happens after a full page refresh? Cypress waits for the new page to finish loading before it runs later commands.

interview.question: What does `cy.go()` yield?

interview.followUp: Can it resolve without a page load? Yes. Hash-based routing and similar navigation can resolve immediately when no page load occurs.

interview.question: When can `cy.go()` time out?

interview.question: What does `cy.hash()` yield?
interview.answer: It returns the active page URL's hash, including `#`. If the URL has no hash value, it yields an empty string.

interview.question: How are query strings handled in hash routes?
interview.answer: A hash route can contain a query string after `#`, and that query remains part of the hash. For example, `#/users/1?tab=profile` is one hash value.
interview.followUp: Which command reads the query before `#`? Use `cy.location('search')`, which returns the URL search part before the hash.

interview.question: Can `cy.hash()` handle cross-origin navigation?

interview.followUp: How do encoded spaces appear? A space is yielded as `%20`; use `decodeURIComponent()` in a retryable `.should()` callback for a readable comparison.

The yielded value uses the browser's serialized URL form. Decode it inside a `.should()` callback when comparing readable text.
Use `cy.hash()`, not a detached or element-chained call.

cy.intercept.explanation: cy.intercept() watches requests that match a URL, method, or route matcher. You can only observe them, return fixed data, change the outgoing request, or change the real response. Give a route an alias, then use cy.wait() to receive its request and response details.

cy.intercept(url)

parameters.name: url

interview.question: What can cy.intercept() do?
interview.answer: cy.intercept() can spy on matching traffic or stub it. A static response returns fixed data, while a route handler can inspect or modify the request and response.
interview.followUp: How can a test wait for the request? Alias the intercept with .as(), then call cy.wait('@alias'). The yielded object contains request and response information.

interview.question: How are requests matched?
interview.answer: A route can match by URL, HTTP method, or a RouteMatcher object. If no method is given, all HTTP methods match.
interview.followUp: How would you match repeated query values? Use a URL regular expression or read them in a route handler with URLSearchParams.getAll().

interview.question: What does an aliased intercept yield?
interview.answer: cy.intercept() itself yields null, but an alias can be used with cy.wait(). Waiting yields the completed request and response cycle, so tests can check request bodies or response status and body.
interview.followUp: How do you inspect several matches? Use cy.get('@alias.all'); numbered forms such as @alias.1 and @alias.2 are also supported, starting at 1.

keyPoints: Use the command to observe traffic or replace and modify network behavior.
A route handler runs for each matching request and can work with the full request-response cycle.
A StaticResponse lets a test return fixed status, headers, body, fixture, delay, or network-error behavior.
Alias a route and wait for it to finish before making assertions.
Use the .all suffix to inspect every request captured by an aliased route.
Waiting on an alias array supports several requests at once, and results keep the input alias order.
gotchas: Leaving out the method matches every HTTP method, not only GET requests.
When using numbered aliases, start with 1. Index 0 does not work.
Use numbered or .all aliases with cy.get(), not with cy.wait().
Create the intercept again in each test that needs it.

cy.invoke.summary: invoke() calls a function on the previous Cypress subject and yields its return value. It supports arguments, nested function paths, and array indexes, but repeated retries can call the function more than once.
cy.invoke.explanation: invoke() calls a function on the value yielded by the previous Cypress command and yields that function's return value. You can pass arguments, use a numeric array index, or use dot notation for nested functions. Cypress may call the function again while retrying assertions, so stop the chain after functions that change state.

parameters.name: functionName
parameters.description: Function name, nested dot path, or numeric array index.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Controls logging and timeout. It comes before functionName.

parameters.name: args...
parameters.description: Values passed to the invoked function in order.

cy.invoke.returns: The return value of the invoked function.

example.title: Handle a promise-returning function
example.code:
const userApi = {
  fetchUser: () => Promise.resolve({ name: 'Jane' }),
}

cy.wrap(userApi)
  .then((api) => api.fetchUser())
  .its('name')
  .should('eq', 'Jane')
example.explanation: Use then() for a function that returns a promise. It waits for the promise before reading the result.

interview.question: What does invoke() do?
interview.answer: invoke() calls a named function on the previous command's yielded subject and yields the function's return value. It can also pass arguments after the function name.
interview.followUp: How do you call a nested function? Use a dot-notation path such as invoke('math.sum', 2, 3).

interview.question: Why can invoke() run a function more than once?
interview.answer: invoke() is retried when chained assertions are not yet passing. This means the function may run more than once.
interview.followUp: What should you do for a state-changing function? End the chain at invoke() and start a separate Cypress chain.

interview.question: How should promise-returning functions be handled?
interview.answer: invoke() does not wait for a promise returned by the called function. Call the function inside then(), which waits for the promise, and continue from its resolved value.
interview.followUp: How would you read a property from the resolved object? Chain its('property') after then().

keyPoints: Start with a command that yields an object, element, array, or other subject. Then invoke a function on that subject.
Put function arguments after the function name. They are sent to the function in the same order.
Use a path such as math.sum for a nested function. The function runs with its parent object as this.
For an array of functions, pass a number to choose the function by index before any function arguments.
The next Cypress command receives the called function's return value, so assertions can check it.
Cypress retries the call and its assertions until they pass or the command times out.
Use options such as log: false or timeout: 10000 before the function name.
gotchas: invoke() does not wait for a returned promise to resolve. Use then() when the function returns a promise.
A function with side effects can run more than once. End the chain at invoke() when the function changes state.
Use a static alias when you need to keep the value produced at the time it was saved.
Do not call invoke() directly from cy.

interview.question: What does `cy.its()` do?
interview.answer: `.its()` reads a property from the previous command's subject and yields that property value. The property can be a name, number, or nested path.
interview.followUp: How do you read the second item in an array? Use a numeric path segment such as `.its('items.1')` or bracket notation such as `.its('items[1]')`.

interview.question: How is `.its()` different from `.invoke()`?
interview.answer: It does not call function properties. For example, `.its('getNum')` yields the function itself; `.invoke('getNum')` calls it and yields its return value.
interview.followUp: When would `.then()` be better? Use `.then()` for callback logic that is not just one property read or one function call.

interview.question: How does retrying and timeout behavior work?
interview.answer: `.its()` is a query, so Cypress can retry it with earlier queries until chained assertions pass. The default wait uses `defaultCommandTimeout`, and a longer wait can be supplied with the `timeout` option.
interview.followUp: How would you wait up to ten seconds for a startup flag? Use `.its('appReady', { timeout: 10000 }).should('be.true')`.

keyPoints: Use `.its()` to read a property from the value produced by the preceding Cypress command.
The property argument may be a string name, a number index, or a path to nested data.
Use dot notation for nested objects, such as `.its('body.user')`.
Array items can be selected with paths like `items.1` or `items[1]`.
The command passes the selected value to the next Cypress command.
You can continue the chain with assertions or other commands that use the yielded value.
The options object supports `log` and `timeout`; `timeout` controls how long Cypress waits.
gotchas: Use `.invoke()` to call a function. `.its()` only returns the function as a value.
Do not start with `cy.its()`. Chain it after a command that yields a subject.
A missing property can cause Cypress to keep retrying until the command times out, unless the next assertion allows a missing value.

cy.last.summary: Selects the final DOM element from a Cypress subject set. It can be chained with assertions, queries, and actions.
cy.last.explanation: Chain last() from a command that yields DOM elements. Cypress selects the final element in that set, retries the query and chained assertions, and yields the result for more commands.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings object. The documented options are log, which controls Command Log output, and timeout, which controls the retry period.

cy.last.returns: The last DOM element in the supplied set. The result can be used as the subject for further Cypress commands.

interview.question: What does cy.last() do?
interview.answer: last() selects the final DOM element from the set yielded by the previous command. It yields that element, so other Cypress commands can follow it.
interview.followUp: How would you select the final active list item? Use cy.get('li').filter('.active').last().

interview.question: What can cy.last() be chained from?
interview.answer: It must be chained from a command that yields DOM element(s) or a document. Calling cy.last() directly, or chaining it after a command such as getCookies(), is invalid.
interview.followUp: What should you do if the preceding command yields data instead of DOM elements? Transform or query the page so the chain produces DOM elements before calling last().

interview.question: How does Cypress retry cy.last()?
interview.answer: last() is a query. Cypress retries the query until the elements exist and retries chained assertions until they pass. The timeout option controls how long Cypress waits for the query chain.
interview.followUp: How can you wait longer for a late-rendered final element? Pass an option such as last({ timeout: 10000 }).

keyPoints: It returns the final DOM element in the current subject set.
Because it is a query, you can continue the chain with assertions, searches, or actions.
Cypress waits and retries while the required elements are not yet present.
Assertions after last() can cause Cypress to repeat the query until they succeed.
A timeout passed to last() applies to the complete preceding query chain as well.
eq(-1) is an equivalent way to select the final element; use eq() for other indexes.
gotchas: You cannot call last() directly after cy. Start with a command that yields DOM elements.
Commands that yield non-DOM values cannot be followed by last().
Do not pass a selector to last(). Use filter() first when you need the last element matching a selector.
last() chooses one final element in the whole set, unlike :last-child, which can match one element per parent.

cy.location.summary: `cy.location()` reads the active page URL. It returns the whole location object or one URL property, such as pathname, host, or searchParams.
cy.location.explanation: `cy.location()` reads the active page URL through Cypress and returns either a plain object containing URL parts or one selected property. It is a query, so Cypress retries it and any later assertions until they pass or the timeout expires.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Optional URL property name, such as pathname, host, or searchParams. Without it, the command yields the full location object.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings. log controls Command Log output, and timeout controls how long Cypress waits.

cy.location.returns: A plain location object when no key is supplied; otherwise a URL property value, or a URLSearchParams object for searchParams.

interview.question: What does cy.location() yield?
interview.answer: Without a key, it yields a plain object with properties such as href, origin, pathname, search, hash, host, port, protocol, and searchParams. With a key, it yields that property's value; searchParams is a URLSearchParams object.
interview.followUp: How would you read a repeated query parameter? Use cy.location('searchParams') and invoke getAll() for that parameter.

interview.question: When should you use a key instead of the full location object?
interview.answer: Use cy.location('pathname') when only the path matters, or cy.location('searchParams') for named query parameters. This avoids coupling the assertion to the host or to query-parameter order.
interview.followUp: Why is comparing search to a complete string weaker? The same parameters can appear in another order, while named URLSearchParams checks remain order-independent.

interview.question: Can cy.location() check a cross-origin redirect?
interview.answer: Cypress reads the URL through the browser's automation protocol, so cy.location() can verify a cross-origin redirect before cy.origin() is used to interact with the destination page.
interview.followUp: What should happen after checking the destination origin? Wrap commands that interact with that other origin in cy.origin() for that origin.

keyPoints: It can return the full location data or one selected URL part.
Commands can follow it, and Cypress retries it together with chained assertions.
Passing a property name returns its value and fails if that property does not exist.
Use URLSearchParams methods such as get() and getAll() to inspect query values.
The timeout option lets a location assertion wait longer for slow navigation.
Selecting pathname directly is equivalent to reading it with its(), but is clearer in the command log.
gotchas: It checks the browser's current page, not the destination stored in a link. To test a link target, assert on the link's own property.
The returned object has URL values but no navigation methods such as assign() or reload().
For hash routing, parameters after # are part of hash, so search and searchParams do not contain them.

interview.question: What does cy.log() do?
interview.answer: cy.log() adds a message and optional arguments to the Cypress Command Log. The message supports inline Markdown, and the command yields null.
interview.followUp: How would you print the same information in CI? Register a cy.task() task that calls console.log(), then call cy.task() from the test.

interview.question: When should logging happen inside .then()?
interview.answer: Its arguments are evaluated when the test code runs because Cypress queues commands. To log a value created by an earlier command, place cy.log() inside that command's .then() callback.
interview.followUp: Why can a direct log show an old value? The log is queued before the earlier Cypress command executes, so the variable has not been updated yet.

interview.question: How are extra arguments displayed?
interview.answer: cy.log() joins the message and arguments with a comma and a space. Strings, numbers, and booleans display directly; large arrays and objects are summarized in the Command Log, while full values remain available in browser developer tools.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect summarized values? Click the log entry in the Command Log to print its message and arguments to the Developer Tools console.

keyPoints: Use cy.log(message) for a message, or cy.log(message, args...) to include additional values.
The message and string arguments support inline Markdown. HTML tags are shown as plain text.
Large arrays and objects are shortened in the Command Log to keep it readable. Click the entry to inspect the complete values in developer tools.
The command has no timeout behavior and must be chained from cy.
Since version 7.3.0, every argument passed to cy.log() appears in the Command Log.
gotchas: cy.log() does not print to the terminal or CI output. Use cy.task() with a registered task that calls console.log() when terminal output is needed.
A value changed by an earlier Cypress command may be stale when passed directly to cy.log(). Put the logging call inside .then() to use the produced value.
The command yields null, so it cannot provide a value for assertions or later chained work.

interview.question: What is cy.mount()?
interview.answer: cy.mount() is a custom command used for Cypress component testing. It calls the framework-specific mount function, such as the one exported by cypress/react, cypress/vue, or cypress/angular.
interview.followUp: Why prefer a custom command? It avoids importing mount in every test and provides one place for shared providers, plugins, and other setup.

interview.question: How do you create a cy.mount command?
interview.answer: Register it with Cypress.Commands.add() in a support file. The callback receives the component and framework-specific options, then returns the imported mount function.
interview.followUp: How could the command support a React provider? Wrap the component with the provider inside the callback before passing it to mount.

interview.question: How do you make cy.mount() work with TypeScript?
interview.answer: Add a Cypress.Chainable declaration that defines mount with the framework mount function's type. If TypeScript cannot find it, include the declaration file in the relevant tsconfig.json files.
interview.followUp: Where can the declaration live? The documentation recommends a root cypress.d.ts file, or another file explicitly included by tsconfig.json.

keyPoints: Use a custom command instead of importing a mount helper in every component spec.
Put repeated setup, such as providers or plugins, inside the custom command.
Import the mount function that matches your framework, such as cypress/react, cypress/vue, or cypress/angular.
After registration, component tests can call cy.mount() without importing the framework helper.
Declare the command in Cypress.Chainable to get TypeScript checking and editor completion.
gotchas: The command is not built in. Add it in a support file before using cy.mount().
TypeScript needs a declaration that is included by the relevant tsconfig.json files. A root cypress.d.ts file is one documented option.

interview.question: What does `.next()` do?
interview.answer: `cy.next()` gets the immediately following sibling of each element in the current subject. It yields the sibling elements it finds and can be followed by more Cypress commands.
interview.followUp: What does the selector argument do? It filters the immediately following siblings; it does not search through all later siblings.

interview.question: What are the chaining requirements for `.next()`?
interview.answer: The command must be chained from a command that yields DOM elements or a document. Calling it directly from `cy` or after a non-DOM command is invalid.
interview.followUp: How would you move across several following siblings? Use a related traversal command such as `.nextAll()` or `.nextUntil()`, depending on the stopping rule.

interview.question: How can `.next()` be configured?
interview.answer: The optional selector filters the next sibling for each current element. The command also supports `log` and `timeout` options.
interview.followUp: What happens if the sibling is not present immediately? Cypress retries while waiting for the element, and it can also retry until chained assertions pass.

keyPoints: It returns the immediate next sibling for every element in the current subject.
Pass a selector when the next sibling must match a particular CSS selector.
Its sibling-selection behavior follows jQuery's `.next()` behavior.
The command yields the newly found DOM elements for the next command in the chain.
Because it is a query, later Cypress commands can safely use its result.
The `timeout` option controls how long Cypress waits for `.next()` to finish.
gotchas: Do not call `.next()` directly from `cy`; start with a command that yields DOM elements.
Commands that do not yield DOM elements, such as `getCookies()`, cannot be followed by `.next()`.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options that change command behavior. Supported fields include `log` and `timeout`.

cy.not.returns: The remaining DOM element(s) after elements matching the selector are removed.

interview.question: What does Cypress `.not()` do?
interview.answer: `.not()` removes elements that match a CSS selector from the current set. It must be chained from a command that yields DOM elements or a document, and it yields the remaining elements.
interview.followUp: How would you select elements that do not contain text? Use a broad selector followed by `.not(':contains("text")')`; the text match is case-sensitive and uses substring matching.

interview.question: What arguments can `.not()` receive?
interview.answer: The command accepts a selector and an optional options object. The documented options are `log`, which controls command logging, and `timeout`, which controls how long Cypress waits.
interview.followUp: What happens when an assertion follows `.not()`? Cypress retries the query and the chained assertions until they pass or the timeout is reached.

interview.question: Can commands be chained after `.not()`?
interview.answer: `.not()` is a query, so it can be followed by commands and assertions. For example, `.get('ul>li').not('.active').should('have.length', 4)` checks the filtered result.
interview.followUp: When might `.filter(':not(.disabled)')` be preferable? Use it when expressing the selection as a positive filter is clearer and you want to keep elements that satisfy that selector.

keyPoints: Use `.not(selector)` to remove matching elements from an existing DOM collection.
`.not()` performs the opposite selection operation from `.filter()`.
Its selector behavior follows jQuery's `.not()` behavior.
The result is the new collection after matching elements have been removed.
You can continue the Cypress chain after `.not()`.
The command supports a selector and an optional options object.
gotchas: You cannot call `.not()` directly from `cy`, or after a command such as `cy.clock()` that does not yield DOM elements.
When using `:contains(...)`, matching is case-sensitive and checks for a substring.
The command waits for matching DOM elements to exist before continuing.

cy.origin.summary: Use cy.origin() to interact with a page on another origin during the same Cypress test. Put commands for that page in its callback and pass data through the serializable args option.
cy.origin.explanation: Cypress runs commands inside the callback against the origin named by the URL. Values cannot be read directly from the outer test, so pass serializable data with args. The callback can yield a serializable value back to the test. After the callback, commands run against the test's current origin.

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: The secondary origin URL or domain. It must use the matching scheme, hostname, and port, and must differ from the current origin.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional object. Its only supported property is args, a serializable plain object passed to the callback.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: Function whose Cypress commands run on the secondary origin. Its only argument is the deserialized args object.

cy.origin.returns: Yields the last Cypress command's value, or the callback's return value when no Cypress command runs. The value is serialized when it returns to the test.

example.title: Test a cross-origin login
example.code:
cy.visit('https://app.cypress.io')
cy.contains('a', 'Log in').click()

cy.origin('https://auth.cypress.io', () => {
  cy.get('#username').type('jane')
  cy.contains('button', 'Sign in').click()
})

cy.location('pathname').should('eq', '/dashboard')
example.explanation: The test signs in on another origin, then checks the redirected path in the app.

useCases.scenario: An application sends users to an SSO, OAuth, or other identity provider domain.

useCases.title: Test subdomain navigation
useCases.scenario: A link moves from one application subdomain to another.

useCases.title: Check data on another site

interview.question: When should cy.origin() be used?
interview.answer: Use cy.origin(url, callbackFn) when later commands must interact with a page whose scheme, hostname, or port differs from the test's current origin. Put those commands inside the callback.
interview.followUp: What if the page changes origin after a click? Call cy.origin() for the new origin after the navigation, then put the commands for that page inside its callback.

interview.question: How does data enter a cy.origin() callback?
interview.answer: Pass data through the args option. Cypress serializes the plain object and gives it to the callback as its only argument. Values must be serializable.
interview.followUp: How should a secret be handled? Read it inside the callback with cy.env() instead of passing it through args.

interview.question: What does cy.origin() yield?
interview.answer: The command yields the last Cypress command in the callback. If no Cypress command runs, it yields the callback's return value or a resolved Promise value. The yielded value must be serializable.
interview.followUp: How can a later command use the value? Chain then() after cy.origin() and receive the value there.

keyPoints: Use cy.origin() to run Cypress commands on a page at a different origin.
The callback contains the commands that interact with the secondary page.
Use args to pass a serializable plain object into the callback.
A relative cy.visit() inside the callback uses the cy.origin() URL as its base.
A serializable value can be yielded from the callback and used by the outer test.
For multiple secondary origins, use separate top-level cy.origin() calls in sequence.
gotchas: Only use the args option. Other option keys cause an error.
Do not mix queued Cypress commands with a synchronous truthy return value from the callback.
Cypress cannot automate or communicate with an iframe from another origin.

cy.parent.summary: `cy.parent()` gets the direct parent of the current DOM element set. It moves up one level and can filter the result with a selector.
cy.parent.explanation: `cy.parent()` moves from the current DOM element set to the direct parent elements. It moves up only one level. You can pass a selector to keep only parents that match it. The command retries while waiting for the elements and chained assertions.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: A CSS selector used to filter the direct parent elements.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options that change command behavior. Supported options include `log` and `timeout`.

cy.parent.returns: The new direct parent DOM element or elements. The result can be used as the subject for chained commands.

example.title: Get and check a parent element
example.explanation: This gets the parent of the active list item and checks its class.

useCases.title: Check a direct parent
useCases.scenario: Start with a selected element and inspect or assert its containing element.

useCases.title: Filter parent elements
useCases.scenario: Select several elements and keep only their direct parents that match a CSS selector.

useCases.title: Query from the parent
useCases.scenario: Continue a Cypress chain from the returned parent elements.

interview.question: What does `cy.parent()` yield?
interview.answer: It yields the direct parent DOM element or elements of the current subject. It moves up one DOM level, like jQuery `.parent()`.
interview.followUp: How would you move through multiple ancestor levels? Use `.parents()` or `.parentsUntil()` instead.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the selector argument?
interview.answer: The selector filters the direct parents. For example, `.parent('.sub-nav')` yields only parents matching `.sub-nav`.
interview.followUp: What happens if the direct parent does not match? The filtered result does not include that parent, so later commands must handle the empty result according to Cypress command behavior.

interview.question: How does `cy.parent()` handle waiting and timeouts?
interview.answer: The command retries while waiting for the parent elements to exist and while chained assertions pass. Its wait time uses `defaultCommandTimeout` unless a `timeout` option is provided.
interview.followUp: Where should a timeout be configured for an assertion chain? Set it on the command that produces the subject, rather than on the assertion itself.

keyPoints: The command returns direct parents only, not every ancestor.
An optional selector limits the returned parent elements.
An options object can change command behavior.
The `log` option controls whether the command appears in the Command Log.
The `timeout` option controls how long Cypress waits for the command to resolve.
The result is a new set of DOM elements found as parents.
Because it is a query, more Cypress commands can follow it.
gotchas: Do not call `cy.parent()` by itself. Chain it from a command that yields DOM elements or a document.
It checks only the direct parent. Use `.parents()` when you need ancestors at multiple levels.
Do not chain it after commands that do not yield DOM elements, such as `cy.reload()`.

cy.parents.summary: Use `cy.parents()` to find multiple ancestor elements of a DOM subject. Add a selector to keep only matching ancestors.
cy.parents.explanation: Chain `.parents()` from a Cypress command that yields DOM elements or a document. It moves upward through multiple ancestor levels and yields the matching elements. Pass a selector to keep only ancestors that match it. The command can be followed by more Cypress commands and assertions.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: A selector that filters the ancestor elements.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options that change command behavior. Supported options include `log` and `timeout`.

cy.parents.returns: The DOM elements found among the subject's ancestors.

example.title: Find a matching ancestor
example.explanation: This finds the active list item, moves through its ancestors, keeps the one with class `main-nav`, and checks that it exists.

useCases.title: Locate an ancestor container
useCases.scenario: Find a container several levels above a selected element.

useCases.title: Filter ancestors by selector
useCases.scenario: Select one kind of ancestor from many levels.

useCases.title: Assert DOM structure
useCases.scenario: Verify that an element is inside a required page region.

interview.question: How does `.parents()` differ from `.parent()`?
interview.answer: `.parents()` finds ancestors at multiple levels above the current DOM elements. Unlike `.parent()`, it does not stop after one level.
interview.followUp: How can you limit the result? Pass a selector, such as `.parents('.main-nav')`, to keep only matching ancestors.

interview.question: What can `.parents()` be chained from?
interview.answer: It must be chained from a command that yields DOM elements or a document. Calling it directly from `cy` is invalid.
interview.followUp: What should be used to start the chain? A DOM-querying command such as `cy.get()` can provide the required subject.

interview.question: What does `.parents()` yield, and how does it handle assertions?
interview.answer: The command yields the ancestor DOM elements it finds. Because it is a query, later Cypress commands and assertions can be chained safely.
interview.followUp: What happens if an assertion does not pass immediately? Cypress retries the query and chained assertions until they pass or the timeout is reached.

keyPoints: It searches through multiple ancestor levels, while `.parent()` checks only the direct parent.
An optional selector filters the ancestors returned by the command.
The result is the set of ancestor elements found by the query.
You can continue the Cypress chain after `.parents()`.
The command uses `defaultCommandTimeout` unless a different timeout is supplied.
gotchas: Do not call `cy.parents()` by itself. Start with a command such as `cy.get()` that yields DOM elements.
Commands that do not yield DOM elements cannot be followed by `.parents()`.

cy.pause.summary: `cy.pause()` stops Cypress commands so you can inspect the application in the Cypress app. You can resume all commands or step through them one at a time.
cy.pause.explanation: Cypress queues commands and runs them later. `cy.pause()` stops command execution in the Cypress app, where you can resume everything or run commands one at a time. It passes through the current subject, but DOM subjects should not be used for further chained commands after the pause.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options that change the default behavior. The documented option is `log`, which defaults to `true` and controls whether the command appears in the Command Log.

cy.pause.returns: The same subject that was passed to `.pause()`.

example.title: Pause and inspect a test
example.explanation: The test pauses before the next command. Use the Cypress app to resume all commands or step through them.

useCases.title: Inspect application state
useCases.scenario: A test behaves unexpectedly and you need to inspect the page before later commands run.

useCases.title: Step through commands
useCases.scenario: Several clicks or other actions must be checked individually.

useCases.title: Pause at a chain point
useCases.scenario: A command chain has reached the state you want to examine in the Cypress app.

interview.question: What does `cy.pause()` do?
interview.answer: `cy.pause()` stops Cypress commands so you can inspect the application in the Cypress app. You can resume all commands or step through the next commands from the Command Log.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect a subject during execution? Use `.debug()` in a command chain; the current subject is exposed as `subject` in Developer Tools.

interview.question: How is `cy.pause()` chained and what does it yield?
interview.answer: It can start a chain from `cy` or follow another Cypress command. It yields the same subject it received and cannot time out.
interview.followUp: What should you avoid after pausing a DOM subject? Avoid chaining commands that depend on that DOM element.

interview.question: Does `cy.pause()` run assertions?
interview.answer: `cy.pause()` is a utility command and does not run assertions. Assertions pass through as if the pause were not present.
interview.followUp: How can a test run one command at a time? Place `cy.pause()` in the test, then use the Cypress app to step through commands.

keyPoints: It stops Cypress commands and lets you interact with the application under test.
The Cypress app can resume the whole queue or execute the next command step by step.
You can call it directly from `cy` or append it to another command chain.
The command passes through the subject it receives.
A pause has no timeout condition.
gotchas: This command does not perform assertions. Any existing assertions pass through it.
Do not continue a chain that depends on a DOM element after pausing.
Use `.debug()` when you need a browser debugger breakpoint; `.pause()` controls Cypress command execution instead.

cy.prev.summary: cy.prev() gets the immediately previous sibling of each current DOM element. An optional selector filters the result.
cy.prev.explanation: Use cy.prev() after a command that yields DOM elements. Cypress finds the immediately previous sibling for each element and yields the result, so more Cypress commands can follow. You can pass a selector to keep only previous siblings that match it.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: Optional CSS selector used to filter the previous sibling elements.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings object. Supported options are log and timeout.

cy.prev.returns: The new DOM element or elements found immediately before the current subject.

example.title: Get the previous sibling
example.explanation: This finds the list item immediately before the active item.

useCases.title: Find the previous sibling
useCases.scenario: A list or table row needs the item directly before a selected element.

useCases.title: Filter the previous sibling
useCases.scenario: The previous sibling must have a particular class or tag.

useCases.title: Continue with the yielded element
useCases.scenario: A follow-up assertion or command should run on the preceding element.

interview.question: What does cy.prev() do?
interview.answer: It gets the immediately preceding sibling of each element in the current subject and yields the found DOM element or elements. A selector can limit which previous siblings are accepted.
interview.followUp: How would you use it? Start with a DOM-yielding command such as cy.get('li.active'), then call .prev('.some-class') if filtering is needed.

interview.question: What can cy.prev() be chained from?
interview.answer: It must be chained from a command that yields DOM elements or a document. It cannot be called directly from cy or after a command such as cy.getCookies() that does not yield DOM elements.
interview.followUp: What should replace a non-DOM subject? Use a command that queries the page, such as cy.get(), before calling .prev().

interview.question: What arguments and options does cy.prev() support?
interview.answer: The selector argument filters the immediately preceding siblings. The options object supports log and timeout; timeout controls how long Cypress waits for the query and its assertions.
interview.followUp: When should timeout be changed? Increase it only when the page needs more time to produce the expected DOM state.

keyPoints: It returns the sibling directly before each current element.
Pass a selector when the previous sibling must match a specific CSS pattern.
The command yields the matching DOM elements it finds.
Because it is a query, you can continue the chain with other Cypress commands.
The log option is enabled by default and controls whether the command appears in the Command Log.
gotchas: Start .prev() from a command that yields DOM elements or a document. Calling cy.prev() directly fails.
The command follows jQuery's previous-sibling query behavior.
The query can time out while waiting for matching elements or chained assertions.

cy.readFile.summary: cy.readFile() reads a file from disk and yields its contents. It can reread the file while chained queries or assertions are not passing, so it works well for downloads and files created during a test.
cy.readFile.explanation: Cypress resolves the path from the project root, reads the file, and yields its contents. It reads the file again when chained queries or assertions do not pass, which lets tests wait for files to appear or change. JSON files are parsed unless the encoding is null.
cy.readFile.syntax:
cy.readFile(filePath)
cy.readFile(filePath, encoding)
cy.readFile(filePath, options)
cy.readFile(filePath, encoding, options)

parameters.name: filePath
parameters.description: File path relative to the project root, or an absolute path.

parameters.name: encoding
parameters.description: Encoding such as utf8, base64, hex, or null for a Cypress.Buffer.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options including encoding, log, and timeout.

cy.readFile.returns: Yields the file contents. JSON files are parsed into JavaScript unless encoding is null; null yields a Cypress.Buffer.

example.title: Wait for a downloaded file
example.explanation: This clicks an export control, then waits for the CSV file and checks its contents.

useCases.title: Check downloaded files
useCases.scenario: A test triggers a download and must wait for the file to appear before checking it.

useCases.title: Check generated logs
useCases.scenario: An application or server writes a log during the test and the test checks new content.

useCases.title: Read with a chosen encoding
useCases.scenario: A test needs binary data, base64 text, or the exact raw text of a JSON file.

useCases.title: Reuse data for uploads
useCases.scenario: A file input needs the contents of a file already read by the test.

interview.question: What does cy.readFile() do?
interview.answer: cy.readFile() reads a file relative to the project root and yields its contents. It retries reading until chained queries and assertions pass or the timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: How would you wait for a download? Click the download control, then call cy.readFile() with a path under the configured downloads folder and assert on its contents.

interview.question: How does encoding affect the yielded value?
interview.answer: The default encoding is utf8. A .json file is parsed into a JavaScript value, while null returns a Cypress.Buffer regardless of the extension.
interview.followUp: How can you check JSON formatting exactly? Read it with null, then call toString() on the returned buffer.

interview.question: How does cy.readFile() differ from cy.fixture()?
interview.answer: cy.readFile() reads from the project root and retries on every call. cy.fixture() reads from fixturesFolder, caches the result, and does not retry.
interview.followUp: When is cy.task() better? Use it for large files or work that needs Node.js, returning only the needed result.

keyPoints: filePath is resolved from the project root, which is the directory containing the Cypress configuration file. Absolute paths are also supported.
Pass null as the encoding to receive a Cypress.Buffer, even when the file has a known extension.
The command rereads the file when a later query or assertion in the chain fails.
Files ending in .json are parsed into JavaScript values unless null encoding is used.
As a query, it retries until all chained queries and assertions succeed or the timeout expires.
The command is shown in the Cypress Command Log, and its entry can be opened to inspect console details.
gotchas: A missing file is retried, but another read error, such as invalid JSON, fails immediately.
Use cy.task() when a file may be absent and the test should continue without a failure.
The encoding in options is ignored if encoding is also supplied as the second argument.
A .json file is parsed automatically; use null encoding when you need its raw bytes or exact text.

cy.reload.summary: Reloads the current page and waits for it to finish loading. Pass true to reload without using the cache, or pass options to control logging and timeout.
cy.reload.explanation: Cypress reloads the current page and waits for its load event. You can pass true to avoid the browser cache, or an options object to control logging and the timeout. The command yields the window after loading, but Cypress warns against chaining commands that depend on that yielded window.

parameters.name: forceReload
parameters.description: When true, reloads the current page without using the cache.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Controls command logging and the wait time. log defaults to true; timeout defaults to pageLoadTimeout.

cy.reload.returns: The window object after the page finishes loading.

example.title: Reload and check the page
example.explanation: This visits an admin page, reloads it, and then checks an element after loading.

useCases.title: Reload the current page
useCases.scenario: Refresh the current application state as if the user selected the browser refresh action.

useCases.title: Force a cache-free reload
useCases.scenario: Ensure the browser does not reuse cached resources during a reload.

useCases.title: Check the reloaded page
useCases.scenario: Wait for a page reload, then verify that content or controls are present.

interview.question: What does cy.reload() do?
interview.answer: cy.reload() reloads the current page and waits for the page to finish loading. It yields the window object after loading.
interview.followUp: What response conditions must hold? The response must be text/html and have a 2xx status after redirects; its load event must eventually fire.

interview.question: How do you force a reload without the cache?
interview.answer: Pass true as the first argument to reload without using the browser cache. For example, use cy.reload(true).
interview.followUp: How can you change waiting time without forcing a cache-free reload? Pass an options object, such as { timeout: 20000 }.

interview.question: What options can cy.reload() accept?
interview.answer: The options object supports log, which defaults to true, and timeout, which defaults to pageLoadTimeout. Timeout controls how long Cypress waits for reload to resolve.
interview.followUp: Does a larger timeout guarantee success? No. Network requests can still time out because of operating-system limits.

keyPoints: Use cy.reload(true) when the page must reload without its cache.
The timeout option sets how long Cypress waits for the reload command to finish.
After loading finishes, the command yields the page's window object.
Assertions chained after reload are retried until they pass or time out.
Call reload from the Cypress cy object, not as a standalone function.
gotchas: Do not use later commands that depend on the window yielded by reload.
The reload response must have the content type text/html.
After redirects, the response must have a 2xx status code.
The command can time out if the page never fires its load event.

cy.request.summary: cy.request() sends an HTTP request from a Cypress test and yields its response. Use it to test APIs, seed data, authenticate, or combine API checks with UI tests.
cy.request.explanation: Cypress sends cy.request() through its Node.js process, not through the browser. The command returns an object with the HTTP result, parsed body, headers, timing, and request details. Browser CORS rules do not apply, while cookies are shared with the browser.
cy.request.syntax:
cy.request(url)
cy.request(url, body)
cy.request(method, url)
cy.request(method, url, body)
cy.request(options)

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: The target URL. A relative URL is resolved using Cypress's documented origin order.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description: Data sent in the request. Objects and booleans are JSON-serialized; FormData is sent as multipart/form-data.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: The HTTP method. GET is used when it is omitted.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options such as headers, qs, authentication, timeout, redirect handling, encoding, and retry behavior.

cy.request.returns: Yields a response object containing status, statusText, isOkStatusCode, body, headers, duration, requestHeaders, allRequestResponses, and redirect details when applicable.

example.explanation: This sends a JSON request, then checks the status and returned user.

useCases.title: Log in through an API
useCases.scenario: Submit login requests and reuse the resulting browser cookies.

useCases.title: Test API behavior
useCases.scenario: Check status codes, validation errors, headers, and response bodies directly.

useCases.title: Combine API and UI tests
useCases.scenario: Use an API call to prepare state, then verify that state in the UI.

interview.question: What does cy.request() do?
interview.answer: cy.request() sends a real HTTP request from Cypress's Node.js process and yields a response object. It can be used to test API endpoints, create test data, or authenticate without loading a page.
interview.followUp: Can cy.intercept() stub this request? No. cy.request() does not use browser traffic, so cy.intercept() cannot spy on or stub it.

interview.question: How does cy.request() handle redirects and error statuses?
interview.answer: By default, Cypress follows redirects and fails the test for status codes outside the 2xx and 3xx ranges. Set followRedirect: false to inspect a redirect, or failOnStatusCode: false to assert on an error response.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect the destination of a redirect? With followRedirect: false, read response.redirectedToUrl; response.status contains the redirect status.

interview.question: How are request bodies handled?
interview.answer: Object and boolean bodies are JSON-serialized and receive an application/json Content-Type unless headers override it. String bodies are sent unchanged, without an automatic content type.
interview.followUp: How do you upload a file? Pass a FormData object as body; Cypress sends multipart/form-data with the needed boundary.

keyPoints: Relative URLs use the cy.origin() origin first, then baseUrl, then the visited page.
You can provide only a URL, or specify a method and body for other HTTP operations.
Headers are sent on redirects too, except for the documented redirect exceptions.
retryOnNetworkFailure can retry temporary network failures up to four times.
The yielded response includes status, status text, body, headers, duration, request headers, and redirect information.
Use binary or base64 encoding when a response contains file data rather than ordinary text.
gotchas: Use failOnStatusCode: false when the test must inspect an error response instead of failing immediately.
cy.intercept() does not observe cy.request() because the request does not pass through browser traffic.
A JSON request body does not guarantee a parsed response. The response Content-Type controls body parsing.

cy.root.summary: `cy.root()` yields the current root DOM element. It returns `<html>` by default, or the element scoped by `.within()`.
cy.root.explanation: `cy.root()` gets the current root DOM element. Normally, this is the `<html>` element. Inside a `.within()` callback, it is the element passed to `.within()`. The command is a query, so more Cypress commands can follow it.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings that change command behavior. Supported settings include `log` and `timeout`.

cy.root.returns: The current root DOM element: `<html>` by default, or the element scoped by `.within()`.

example.title: Submit the current within element
example.explanation: Inside the callback, `cy.root()` yields the form, so `submit()` submits that form.

useCases.scenario: Get the document root

useCases.title: Act on an element inside `.within()`
useCases.scenario: Use the current scoped element

useCases.title: Add assertions to the yielded root
useCases.scenario: Check the current scope

interview.question: What element does `cy.root()` yield?
interview.answer: By default, `cy.root()` yields the `<html>` element. It yields a different element when called inside a `.within()` callback.
interview.followUp: What does it yield inside `cy.get('form').within(() => {})`? It yields the form element used by `.within()`.

interview.question: Can commands be chained after `cy.root()`?
interview.answer: Yes. Cypress documents `cy.root()` as a query, so additional commands can be chained after it. For example, a form yielded inside `.within()` can be followed by `.submit()`.
interview.followUp: How can you assert the yielded element? Chain an assertion such as `.should('match', 'html')` or `.should('have.class', 'query-ul')`.

interview.question: When is `cy.root()` useful inside `.within()`?
interview.answer: Use `cy.root()` inside `.within()` when the test needs to act on the element that defines the current scope. For example, calling `.submit()` after it submits the scoped form.
interview.followUp: What happens if it is called outside `.within()`? It yields the document's `<html>` root by default.

keyPoints: The command returns the current root DOM element.
Outside a scoped `.within()` callback, the default root is `<html>`.
Inside `.within()`, the command uses the element currently being scoped.
You can continue the Cypress chain after calling `cy.root()`.
Cypress retries the query while chained assertions are still failing.
gotchas: Call `cy.root()` from the Cypress `cy` object. It cannot be used as an unchained standalone function.
A timeout can happen when chained assertions do not pass before the configured command timeout.

interview.question: What can cy.screenshot() capture?
interview.answer: It captures a PNG and saves it in the screenshots folder. Without a chained element, the default capture is the application page; an element chain captures that element, while capture can select viewport, fullPage, or runner.
interview.followUp: How would you protect sensitive content in failure screenshots? Use onBeforeScreenshot and onAfterScreenshot defaults to hide and then restore sensitive elements, because failure images are runner captures and blackout does not apply.

interview.question: How are screenshot files named and replaced?
interview.answer: The fileName argument names the image relative to the screenshots folder and spec path. A path in the name causes Cypress to create the needed folders.
interview.followUp: How can a baseline always be replaced? Pass overwrite: true for that screenshot.

interview.question: What does cy.screenshot() yield?
interview.answer: The command yields the same subject it received, so an element screenshot can be followed by a command while that element remains in the DOM. Cypress does not query the element again after the screenshot.
interview.followUp: What should you do if the application may replace the element? Query it again with cy.get() before the next command.

keyPoints: It saves a PNG record of the application state at that point in the test.
Use fullPage, viewport, element, or runner capture depending on the needed image.
By default, Cypress pauses timers and CSS animations during capture.
For element screenshots, padding can be one number or CSS-shorthand values for different sides.
The capture option controls whether the image contains the viewport, full page, or runner.
The default output directory is cypress/screenshots; configure screenshotsFolder to change it.

Blackout does not protect content in runner captures, including automatic failure screenshots.
A run removes all files and subfolders in the screenshots folder unless trashAssetsBeforeRuns is disabled.

cy.scrollIntoView.explanation: Chain this command from a Cypress command that yields DOM elements. Cypress scrolls until the subject is visible, then returns that same subject. Use options to control animation, easing, offsets, logging, or timeout. Run a separate assertion after scrolling when you need to verify the result.

parameters.name: options

cy.scrollIntoView.returns: Yields the same subject it received: the selected DOM element(s).

useCases.scenario: An element should appear below a fixed header after scrolling.
