interview.question: How do you scroll an element into view?
interview.answer: Use `cy.get('selector').scrollIntoView()`. The command must be chained from a command that yields DOM element(s); it cannot be called directly from `cy` or from a command yielding `window`.
interview.followUp: How would you verify the result? Start a new query and use an assertion such as `cy.get('selector').should('be.visible')`.

interview.question: How can you change the scrolling behavior?
interview.answer: Pass an options object. `duration` controls the animation time in milliseconds, `easing` controls the animation style, and `offset` adds a final top and left scroll amount.
interview.followUp: How do you place an element 150 pixels below the top position? Use `{ offset: { top: 150, left: 0 } }`.

interview.question: What is the difference between `scrollIntoView()` and `scrollTo()`?
interview.answer: `.scrollIntoView()` scrolls until a target element is in view. `.scrollTo()` instead scrolls a container, such as the window or a scrollable element, to a position.
interview.followUp: When is explicit scrolling useful? Use it when a test needs to exercise scrolling or when content appears progressively during scrolling.

keyPoints: Use the command to bring a selected DOM element into the visible area.
An options object lets you customize how the scroll is performed.
Set `duration` to control how long the scroll animation takes.
Set `easing` to choose the animation curve, such as `linear`.
Use `offset` with `top` and `left` values to adjust the final position.
Follow-up assertions can retry until they succeed or the configured timeout is reached.
gotchas: The command yields the original subject, but relying on that subject in later chained commands is unsafe. Start a new query for follow-up checks.
The scroll action runs only once. Assertions added after it can retry until they pass or time out.
Cypress snapshots do not show the real scroll position. Use pause or watch the test video to inspect scrolling.

cy.scrollTo.summary: cy.scrollTo() moves the window or a scrollable element to a named position or coordinate. It supports pixel and percentage values, animation options, and a scrollability check.
cy.scrollTo.explanation: Use cy.scrollTo() to move the window or one scrollable element to a named position or coordinate. It waits for the target to be attached and scrollable, then performs one scroll; assertions after it can retry.
cy.scrollTo.syntax:
cy.scrollTo(position)
cy.scrollTo(x, y)
cy.scrollTo(position, options)
cy.scrollTo(x, y, options)
.scrollTo(position)
.scrollTo(x, y)
.scrollTo(position, options)
.scrollTo(x, y, options)

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: A named destination: topLeft, top, topRight, left, center, right, bottomLeft, bottom, or bottomRight.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Horizontal distance from the left edge, as pixels or a percentage.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Vertical distance from the top edge, as pixels or a percentage.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options such as duration, easing, ensureScrollable, and log.

cy.scrollTo.returns: .scrollTo() yields the same subject it was given. A standalone cy.scrollTo() yields the window.

example.title: Load more items
example.explanation: Scrolls the feed to its end, then waits for more items to appear.

useCases.title: Reach a container position
useCases.scenario: Move a page or panel to its end, edge, or center before checking its content.

useCases.title: Load more list items
useCases.scenario: Scroll an infinite list so the application loads another page of items.

useCases.title: Trigger scroll-based UI
useCases.scenario: Reveal UI such as a back-to-top button, sticky header, or lazy image.

interview.question: What does cy.scrollTo() scroll?
interview.answer: It scrolls the window when used as cy.scrollTo(), or a selected scrollable element when chained from cy.get(). It accepts named positions or horizontal and vertical coordinates.
interview.followUp: How would you verify the result? Query scrollY on the window or scrollTop on the element after the scroll.

interview.question: Which destinations and coordinate formats are supported?
interview.answer: Named positions include topLeft, top, topRight, left, center, right, bottomLeft, bottom, and bottomRight. Coordinates can be numbers, pixel strings, or percentages.
interview.followUp: What is the difference from scrollIntoView()? scrollTo() moves a container to a position, while scrollIntoView() moves until a specific element is visible.

interview.question: Which options change scrolling behavior?
interview.answer: The default duration is 0, easing is swing, ensureScrollable is true, and log is true. Set duration or easing for animation, or set ensureScrollable to false to skip the scrollability check.
interview.followUp: When should ensureScrollable be false? Use it when an element is scrollable only in some application states, such as a table with varying row counts.

keyPoints: It can scroll either the browser window or a scrollable element.
Named destinations cover the corners, edges, and center of the scroll area.
Coordinates accept pixel numbers, pixel strings, or percentages.
Use duration to animate the scroll for a specified number of milliseconds.
The easing option accepts swing or linear.
A standalone call yields the window; a chained call yields the subject it scrolled.
gotchas: Do not depend on the subject after scrolling. Query the window or element again before checking its scroll position.
The target must contain exactly one element.
A non-scrollable target causes an error by default. Disable this check only when the target may sometimes be non-scrollable.
The scroll itself runs once, but later assertions can retry while the page updates.

cy.select.summary: cy.select() chooses one or more options in a <select> element by value, index, or text. It supports action options such as force, log, and timeout.
cy.select.explanation: Chain select() from a command that yields a DOM element containing a select element. Give one value, index, or option text for one choice, or an array for multiple choices. Cypress waits for the select to become actionable and retries chained assertions.
cy.select.syntax:
cy.get('select').select(value)
cy.get('select').select(values)
cy.get('select').select(value, options)
cy.get('select').select(values, options)

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: An option value, index, or text content. A string or number selects one option.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: Option values, indexes, or text contents to select. An empty array clears all options.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Controls command behavior: force, log, and timeout.

cy.select.returns: The same subject that was passed to select(). The documentation says it is unsafe to chain commands that rely on this subject.

example.title: Select an option by text
example.explanation: This finds a select element, chooses the option whose text is "apples", and checks its value.

useCases.title: Choose one option by text
useCases.scenario: A form has a normal dropdown and the test must choose an option by its displayed label.

useCases.title: Choose several options
useCases.scenario: A multiple select must contain a specific set of choices.

useCases.title: Force selection on a hidden select
useCases.scenario: A select is hidden during a test setup or special UI flow.

interview.question: What can select() use to identify an option?
interview.answer: select() must be chained from a command that yields DOM elements, and the yielded element must be a select. The argument can identify an option by its value, index, or displayed text.
interview.followUp: What happens with an array? It selects only matching options, so previous selections not in the array are removed; [] clears all selections.

interview.question: How does select() handle multiple selections and force mode?
interview.answer: Pass a single string or number for one option, or an array for several options. The array items can be option values, indexes, or text contents.
interview.followUp: Can force: true select a disabled option? No. It does not bypass checks for a disabled option or an option inside a disabled optgroup.

interview.question: How does Cypress wait and retry around select()?
interview.answer: Cypress waits for the select to become actionable and retries chained assertions until they pass or time out. The timeout can be set with the options object's timeout property.
interview.followUp: What subject does select() yield? It yields the same subject it received, but relying on that subject in later commands is unsafe.

keyPoints: A single argument can be an option's value, zero-based index, or visible text.
Use an array to choose several options in a multiple select.
The yielded subject must contain a select element.
Cypress waits until the select can be acted on before selecting.
Assertions after the command are retried until they pass or time out.
The log option controls whether this command appears in Cypress's Command Log.
gotchas: The command yields the original subject, but the documentation warns that later commands should not rely on that subject.
An array replaces the current selection with only matching options. An empty array clears every selection.
force: true can bypass checks for a hidden or disabled select, but not for a disabled option or disabled option group.

cy.session.summary: cy.session() caches and restores cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage. Use it to avoid repeating login setup and to switch between saved user sessions.
cy.session.explanation: Cypress runs setup only when the session ID has no valid cached session. It then saves cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage. Later calls restore that data and run validation when provided. The page is cleared according to testIsolation, while stored browser data is cleared before setup.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Unique cache key. A string can be used directly; arrays and objects are deterministically stringified.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Commands that create the session when it is missing or invalid.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings, including validate and cacheAcrossSpecs.

example.title: Cache an API login
example.explanation: This creates or restores a login session. The validation request makes Cypress recreate it when the saved session is no longer valid.

useCases.title: Reuse a login session
useCases.scenario: Many tests use the same authenticated user.

useCases.title: Switch users without logging out
useCases.scenario: A test changes between two authenticated users.

useCases.title: Share a session across specs
useCases.scenario: Several specs need one shared login during one run.

useCases.title: Recreate invalid sessions
useCases.scenario: A login can expire or become invalid.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the first cy.session() argument?
interview.answer: The ID identifies the cached session. A string works for simple cases, while arrays and objects are deterministically converted into an ID.
interview.followUp: What should distinguish two login methods with different stored data? Include the method name in each ID, such as ['loginByApi', name], so their caches cannot collide.

interview.question: When does setup run?
interview.answer: setup runs for a new or invalid session. Cypress then saves cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage so later calls can restore them without repeating setup.
interview.followUp: What happens after a restored session fails validation? Cypress runs setup again to create a replacement session.

interview.question: How does session validation work?
interview.answer: validate checks a newly created or restored session. A failing Cypress command, rejected promise, false result, or false final command makes the session invalid.
interview.followUp: Where should login success assertions go? Put them inside setup so setup cannot finish and cache an incomplete login.

keyPoints: cy.session() saves and restores the browser data used for a session.
Cypress caches the session after setup and its first validation complete.
With test isolation enabled, Cypress clears the page before setup runs.
The command yields created, restored, or recreated to show what happened.
gotchas: Do not visit the login page before cy.session(). Put the visit inside setup because the page is blank when setup starts.
Avoid large or circular values for the session ID because Cypress must serialize them.
When sharing a session across specs, keep all session arguments identical in every spec.

cy.setCookie.summary: Sets a browser cookie for testing. Use an options object to control its scope, lifetime, security, SameSite behavior, and timeout.
cy.setCookie.explanation: cy.setCookie() asks Cypress to add a browser cookie with a name and value. You can control its domain, expiry, path, security flags, SameSite setting, timeout, and host-only behavior with an options object. Cypress clears cookies between tests by default, so set known values in beforeEach when every test needs them.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Cookie name.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Cookie value.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings, including domain, expiry, hostOnly, httpOnly, path, secure, timeout, and sameSite.

cy.setCookie.returns: Yields a cookie object containing properties such as domain, expiry, hostOnly, httpOnly, path, secure, sameSite, and value.

example.title: Set a cookie before each test
example.explanation: This sets a known cookie before each test, then checks its value.

useCases.title: Set a known cookie in beforeEach
useCases.scenario: A test needs a fixed consent or feature-flag value before it loads the page.

useCases.title: Restore login state with cy.session()
useCases.scenario: Tests need a cookie created by a login flow without logging in every time.

useCases.title: Restrict a cookie to one host
useCases.scenario: A cookie must not be sent to sibling or parent hosts.

interview.question: What does cy.setCookie() do, and which arguments does it accept?
interview.answer: It sets a browser cookie using a required name and value. An optional object changes settings such as domain, path, expiry, security flags, SameSite, and timeout.
interview.followUp: How would you limit the cookie to one host? Pass hostOnly: true, so sibling and parent hosts do not receive it.

interview.question: How can a cookie be preserved across tests?
interview.answer: Cypress clears cookies before each test when test isolation is enabled. Re-create a known cookie in beforeEach when all tests need the same value.
interview.followUp: What should you use for a server-created login cookie? Use cy.session(), which restores cookies and browser storage without repeating the login flow.

interview.question: What is the difference between domain and host-only cookies?
interview.answer: The default cookie is a domain cookie, so it can be sent to matching subdomains. A host-only cookie is restricted to the exact host and uses hostOnly: true.
interview.followUp: Why might a cookie appear on an unexpected cy.request()? The cookie jar sends domain-matching cookies, including to another host on the same registrable domain.

keyPoints: name is the cookie name and must be a string.
value is the cookie value and must be a string.
expiry uses Unix time in seconds; its default is about 20 years in the future.
Set httpOnly: true to prevent normal browser scripts from accessing the cookie.
Set secure: true to mark the cookie as secure.
sameSite accepts lax, strict, or no_restriction; undefined uses the browser default.
gotchas: The default cookie can match subdomains. Use hostOnly: true when the cookie must match only the exact host.
Before visiting a page, the default domain may be the host serving the spec. Pass domain explicitly when setting a cookie for another domain.
For a different origin, run the command inside cy.origin().
The SameSite value no_restriction requires secure: true.

cy.should.summary: Use cy.should() to assert the current Cypress subject. Cypress retries the assertion until it passes or times out.
cy.should.explanation: Cypress runs assertions made by should() again until they pass or the command times out. It normally yields the previous subject, but some chainers yield a new value. A callback can contain several assertions, but Cypress commands cannot run inside that callback.

parameters.name: chainers
parameters.description: A valid Chai, Chai-jQuery, or Sinon-Chai assertion name.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value checked by the chainer.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: The method called on the chainer.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: A callback containing assertions for the yielded subject.

cy.should.returns: Usually yields the subject from the previous command. A chainer can change the subject. A callback's return value is ignored, and the original subject is yielded.

example.title: Retry assertions
example.code:
cy.get('.error').should('be.empty')
cy.get('input').should('have.value', 'ready')
cy.get('button').click()
cy.get('#status').should(($status) => {
  expect($status).to.have.length(1)
  expect($status).to.contain('Done')
})
example.explanation: Use a chainer for a single check. Pass a callback when one subject needs several assertions.

useCases.title: Verify element state
useCases.scenario: Check an element's state, such as visibility, focus, selection, classes, or value.

useCases.title: Compare a value
useCases.scenario: Check a URL, attribute, or property against an expected value.

useCases.title: Group assertions
useCases.scenario: Make several checks on the same yielded element or collection.

interview.question: What does should() do?
interview.answer: should() creates an assertion and retries it until it passes or times out. It can use a chainer, a chainer with a value, a method and value, or a callback.
interview.followUp: How does a callback differ from then()? A should() callback is retried until its assertions stop throwing, while then() is not retried.

interview.question: What does should() yield?
interview.answer: Usually, should() yields the subject received from the previous command. Some chainers, such as have.attr or have.css, change the subject to the selected attribute or CSS value.
interview.followUp: What happens after a subject changes? Later assertions receive the new yielded value, so chain them according to the chainer's documented result.

interview.question: When should you use a callback?
interview.answer: A callback lets you make multiple assertions against one yielded subject. Cypress retries the callback when an assertion throws, ignores its return value, and does not allow Cypress commands inside it.
interview.followUp: How should a command be used after a callback? Chain then() afterward when you need a Cypress command, because the original subject is yielded.

keyPoints: Cypress retries should() assertions until they pass or the timeout is reached.
The chainer can come from Chai, Chai-jQuery, or Sinon-Chai.
Most assertions keep the previous command's subject.
Some chainers replace the subject with a value, such as an attribute or CSS property.
Use and() to add another assertion; it works the same as should().
A callback supports multiple explicit assertions for one subject.
gotchas: Do not call Cypress commands such as cy.log() inside a should() callback. Put them before or after should().
Returning a value from the callback does not change the subject yielded to the next command.
A callback can run more than once, so avoid actions or other side effects inside it.
Do not call should() directly from cy. Chain it from a previous Cypress command.

cy.siblings.summary: Use .siblings() to find sibling DOM elements. Add a selector to filter the results, or options to control logging and timeout.
cy.siblings.explanation: Chain .siblings() after a command that yields DOM elements or a document. Cypress finds the matching sibling elements, can filter them with a selector, and retries the query and later chained assertions until they pass or the timeout is reached.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: A CSS selector that filters the sibling elements returned by the query.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options that change command behavior. Supported options include log and timeout.

cy.siblings.returns: .siblings() yields the new DOM element(s) it found and is safe to chain further commands.

example.title: Find sibling elements
example.explanation: The first query finds the other list items beside the active item. The second query filters the siblings to the active item.

useCases.title: Get all siblings
useCases.scenario: Find the other items in a list beside a selected item.

useCases.title: Filter siblings
useCases.scenario: Check or interact with only siblings matching a CSS selector.

useCases.title: Use retryable queries
useCases.scenario: Wait for sibling elements that appear after page updates.

interview.question: What does cy.siblings() do?
interview.answer: It gets sibling DOM elements for each element in the current subject. An optional selector limits the returned siblings to matching elements.
interview.followUp: What can you chain after it? Because it yields new DOM elements and is a query, further commands and assertions can be chained safely.

interview.question: What are the chaining requirements?
interview.answer: The command must follow a command that yields DOM elements or a document. Calling cy.siblings() directly is invalid.
interview.followUp: Why does cy.clock().siblings() fail? cy.clock() does not yield DOM elements, so there is no valid DOM subject for the query.

interview.question: How can sibling results be filtered and synchronized?
interview.answer: The selector argument filters the sibling elements. For example, cy.get('li').siblings('.active') returns only matching siblings.
interview.followUp: How does Cypress handle delayed elements? It retries until the elements exist and until chained assertions pass, subject to the command timeout.

keyPoints: Use .siblings() to find DOM elements that share a parent with the current elements.
Pass a selector when you need only siblings that match a specific CSS pattern.
An options object can change command behavior, including logging and timeout settings.
The log option controls whether the command appears in Cypress's Command Log.
The timeout option controls how long Cypress waits for the query to resolve.
The command returns the newly found sibling elements.
gotchas: You cannot call .siblings() directly from cy, and the previous command must yield DOM elements or a document.
The query waits for the matching elements to exist before continuing.
A command such as cy.clock() cannot be followed by .siblings().

cy.spy.summary: cy.spy() wraps a function or object method to record calls and arguments. It leaves the original behavior unchanged, so the real function still runs.
cy.spy.explanation: cy.spy() records calls, arguments, and other call details for a function. When given an object and method name, it wraps the method without replacing its original behavior.

parameters.name: object
parameters.description: The object that contains the method to wrap.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: The method name on the object to wrap.

cy.spy.returns: A synchronous Sinon.js spy, not a Promise-like chainable object.

example.title: Spy on a method call
example.explanation: This wraps the method, records the call, and keeps the original method behavior.

useCases.title: Test component events
useCases.scenario: Check that a component callback receives the expected value after a user interaction.

useCases.title: Check internal method calls
useCases.scenario: Verify that one method calls another without blocking the called method's real action.

useCases.title: Observe function behavior
useCases.scenario: Inspect call count, arguments, return value, or invocation context while preserving behavior.

interview.question: What is the difference between a spy and a stub?
interview.answer: cy.spy() observes a function and records calls, arguments, and related details. It does not change the function's behavior, so the original method still runs.
interview.followUp: When would you use cy.stub() instead? Use cy.stub() when you need to control or replace behavior, such as forcing a return value or preventing side effects.

interview.question: How do you create and assert a spy?
interview.answer: For an object method, pass the object and the method name: cy.spy(object, 'method'). For a standalone callback, cy.spy() creates a spy that can be passed to application code.
interview.followUp: How can the spy be retrieved later? Call .as('name'), then use cy.get('@name') for assertions.

interview.question: What does cy.spy() return and which assertions can it use?
interview.answer: cy.spy() returns a Sinon.js spy synchronously. Cypress also provides Sinon-Chai support, so assertions such as called and calledWith can be used.
interview.followUp: How can you reduce command-log noise? Chain .log(false) on the spy.

keyPoints: A spy tracks when a function runs and which arguments it receives.
The returned value supports Sinon.JS spy methods.
Use .as() to give a spy a name and retrieve it later with cy.get().
Use .log(false) when frequent spy calls make the Command Log noisy.
Sinon-Chai assertions work without extra configuration.
gotchas: It is synchronous, not chainable, retryable, or timeout-able.
Use a spy when the real method should still run; use a stub when its behavior must be replaced.
Do not add manual reset or restore code between tests.

cy.stub.summary: cy.stub() replaces a function with a Sinon stub. It records calls and lets you control the function's behavior, such as its return value or thrown error.
cy.stub.explanation: cy.stub() replaces a function with a Sinon stub. The stub records calls and lets the test control results, arguments, callbacks, or errors. It returns immediately, so it is not a chainable Cypress command. Cypress resets and restores stubs between tests.

parameters.name: object
parameters.description: The object whose method will be replaced.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: The name of the method to replace.

cy.stub.returns: A synchronous Sinon.js stub. It is not a Promise-like chainable object.

example.title: Replace a method and control its result
example.explanation: This replaces api.save, controls its result, records the call, and checks the stub.

useCases.title: Prevent side effects
useCases.scenario: A function causes navigation or another unwanted side effect.

useCases.title: Control asynchronous results
useCases.scenario: A Promise must resolve or reject predictably.

useCases.title: Force test paths
useCases.scenario: The test needs to exercise success and failure paths.

useCases.title: Test callback behavior
useCases.scenario: A callback must be invoked by the test double.

interview.question: What does cy.stub() do?
interview.answer: cy.stub() replaces a function and returns a Sinon stub. The stub records calls, and methods such as returns(), callsFake(), resolves(), and rejects() control its behavior.
interview.followUp: When should cy.spy() be used instead? Use it when calls must be observed but the original method should continue to run.

interview.question: What are the supported cy.stub() signatures?
interview.answer: The two forms are cy.stub() for a standalone stub and cy.stub(object, method) to replace a method on an object. The result is synchronous and can be aliased.
interview.followUp: How can a later assertion retrieve the stub? Give it an alias with as(), then use cy.get('@alias').

interview.question: When should a window method be stubbed?
interview.answer: In end-to-end tests, built-in window methods must be stubbed in the onBeforeLoad callback passed to cy.visit(). In component tests, stub the function before mounting the component.
interview.followUp: Why does timing matter? The application may capture or call the original method during startup, before a later stub can replace it.

keyPoints: A stub replaces a function, records how it is used, and lets the test choose its behavior.
The returned value is a Sinon stub, so Sinon stub methods and Cypress assertions for calls are available.
Stub functions with side effects when the test needs predictable success, failure, callbacks, or promise results.
Use .as('name') to label a stub and later retrieve it with cy.get('@name').
Cypress automatically resets and restores stubs between tests, so explicit cleanup is normally unnecessary.
Call .log(false) when frequent stub calls would make the Command Log too noisy.
gotchas: Do not treat cy.stub() as a chainable Cypress command or wait for it with a command timeout.
For end-to-end tests, stub browser methods in cy.visit()'s onBeforeLoad callback, before the application loads.
Use cy.spy() when the original function must still run; use cy.stub() when its behavior must change.

cy.submit.explanation: Chain `.submit()` from a Cypress command that yields a form element. Cypress submits the form directly, but the command is not an action command, so it does not use the usual actionability waiting rules. Client-side validation errors make the command fail.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options object. `log` defaults to `true`; `timeout` defaults to `defaultCommandTimeout`.

cy.submit.returns: The same subject that was passed to `.submit()`. Chaining commands that rely on this subject is unsafe.

example.title: Submit one form
example.explanation: Select the form by its ID, then submit that single form.

useCases.title: Submit a specific form
useCases.scenario: Submit a form selected by a stable ID or other selector.

useCases.title: Customize command behavior
useCases.scenario: Hide the command from the Cypress Command Log or change its wait limit.

interview.question: What subject does `.submit()` require?
interview.answer: `.submit()` submits a form selected by a previous Cypress command. The previous command must yield a form element, and the form must be a single form.
interview.followUp: What happens if the selector yields an input? Cypress errors because the subject is not a form.

interview.question: What does `.submit()` yield?
interview.answer: The command yields the same subject it received. However, Cypress marks it unsafe to chain commands that rely on that subject afterward.
interview.followUp: Why might a later assertion be unreliable? The subject after submission may no longer represent a safe basis for dependent commands.

interview.question: Is `.submit()` an action command?
interview.answer: `.submit()` is a shortcut for submitting a form without clicking a submit button or typing Enter. It does not use the normal actionability-waiting rules.
interview.followUp: When should another command be used? Use `.click()` or `.type()` when actionability waiting is needed.

keyPoints: Use `.submit()` to submit a form directly.
Chain the command from a subject that is a form element.
You can pass an options object to control logging and timeout behavior.
The `log` option defaults to `true` and controls whether Cypress displays the command in its Command Log.
The `timeout` option uses `defaultCommandTimeout` unless you provide another value.
Assertions chained to the command are retried until they pass or time out.
gotchas: Do not chain later commands that depend on the form subject after submitting.
The command must target one form, not multiple forms.
Invalid client-side form fields cause submission to fail and show the validation failures.
Do not expect the actionability waiting behavior used by commands such as `.click()`.

cy.task.summary: cy.task() runs a named handler in Node.js from a Cypress test. Use it for work the browser cannot do, such as database access and file-system operations.
cy.task.explanation: cy.task() sends a named event from browser-side test code to a handler registered in setupNodeEvents. The handler runs in Node.js, so it can access files, databases, command-line tools, and other resources unavailable in the browser. Arguments and results are serialized, and the handler must return a value, a promise, or null.
cy.task.syntax:
cy.task(event)
cy.task(event, arg)
cy.task(event, arg, options)

parameters.name: event
parameters.description: The task event name handled by setupNodeEvents.

parameters.name: arg
parameters.description: Optional JSON-serializable value sent to the handler. Use an object for multiple values.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings: log controls command logging; timeout controls how long Cypress waits, using taskTimeout by default.

cy.task.returns: Yields the value returned by, or resolved by, the task handler in setupNodeEvents.

example.title: Run Node.js code from a test
example.explanation: The test calls a task, and the handler runs in Node.js and returns the result.

useCases.title: Seed a database
useCases.scenario: Prepare server-side data before a test or suite.

useCases.title: Work with files
useCases.scenario: Read, count, remove, or inspect files outside the browser.

useCases.title: Run external processes
useCases.scenario: Run an external CLI or command from a test.

useCases.title: Share run state
useCases.scenario: Keep small values available to later specs in one run.

interview.question: What is cy.task() used for?
interview.answer: cy.task() lets browser-side Cypress code run a named handler in Node.js. Register the handler with on('task', ...) inside setupNodeEvents.
interview.followUp: What happens when the handler is asynchronous? It may return a promise, and cy.task() yields the resolved value; the command fails if that value is undefined.

interview.question: What can you pass to a task?
interview.answer: The event is a string, and the optional argument can be any value JSON.stringify() can serialize. For several values, pass one object and destructure it in the handler.
interview.followUp: How are special values handled? Functions, symbols, and undefined are removed from object properties, while dates become ISO strings.

interview.question: What does cy.task() yield?
interview.answer: The command yields the value returned or resolved by the task handler. Its default timeout is taskTimeout, and it also supports log and timeout options.
interview.followUp: How can a task signal success without returning data? Return null instead of undefined.

keyPoints: Use cy.task() when test code needs Node.js work that the browser cannot perform.
Tasks can seed or query databases, which is useful for preparing and checking server-side test data.
A task can read, remove, inspect, or count files on the machine running Cypress.
A handler may return a direct value or a promise. Cypress waits for the promise before yielding its result.
Pass multiple inputs as one object. Destructure that object in the task handler.
A value kept in the config process can remain available to later spec files during the same run.
gotchas: A task handler must not return undefined. Return null when the operation succeeds but has no result.
Only send JSON-serializable arguments. Circular objects cause the command to fail.
Do not use a task to start a web server. Start the server before Cypress runs.
In parallel runs, task state is not shared between machines or config processes.

cy.then.summary: cy.then() gives a callback the subject from the previous Cypress command. Its return value, a returned Cypress chain, or a resolved Promise controls the subject passed to the next command.
cy.then.explanation: cy.then() runs a callback after the previous Cypress command resolves. The callback receives that command's subject. Its returned value becomes the next subject, including a resolved Promise or returned Cypress chain. Without a non-null return, Cypress uses the last command in the callback, or keeps the previous subject if no Cypress command runs.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings object. The documented timeout controls how long cy.then() waits for its callback to resolve.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: Function that receives the subject yielded by the previous command.

cy.then.returns: The callback result becomes the next subject. A returned Cypress chain or Promise is resolved first. If the callback returns null or undefined, Cypress yields the last command in the callback, or retains the previous subject when no Cypress command ran.

example.title: Use the yielded subject
example.explanation: The callback receives the button yielded by cy.get(). It can read the element and queue more Cypress commands.

useCases.title: Transform a subject
useCases.scenario: Read or transform a yielded value before continuing the chain.

useCases.title: Use the current subject
useCases.scenario: Run code that needs the resolved subject, such as inspecting an element or choosing the next command.

useCases.title: Integrate a Promise
useCases.scenario: Wait for an external Promise and continue with its resolved value.

useCases.title: Prefer should() instead
useCases.scenario: Perform assertions that must be retried until they pass.

interview.question: How does cy.then() determine the next subject?
interview.answer: The callback gets the subject yielded by the previous command. A non-null return becomes the next subject. If it returns nothing, Cypress uses the last Cypress command in the callback, or preserves the prior subject when no Cypress command ran.
interview.followUp: What happens when the callback returns a Promise? Cypress waits for the Promise to resolve and uses the resolved value as the next subject.

interview.question: What is the difference between cy.then() and a callback passed to should()?
interview.answer: cy.then() runs its callback once. A callback passed to .should() or .and() can run again until its assertions stop throwing, so .should() is the better choice for retryable assertions.
interview.followUp: Why can side effects in a .should() callback be risky? The callback may run multiple times, so an action could happen more than once.

interview.question: Why must conditional logic use the Cypress command flow?
interview.answer: Cypress commands are queued and execute later in order. JavaScript outside the command chain can run before queued commands, so dependent logic belongs inside cy.then() or another Cypress command callback.
interview.followUp: Why is a while loop a poor way to repeat Cypress work? It keeps queuing commands before Cypress can execute them; recursion lets the current chain run before adding more commands.

keyPoints: The callback receives the previous command's yielded subject as its first argument.
A returned non-null value becomes the subject passed to the next command.
Returning a Cypress chain makes Cypress wait for that chain and use its result as the next subject.
A returned Promise pauses the chain until it resolves; its resolved value becomes the next subject.
No explicit value means Cypress can yield the last command run inside the callback.
Use cy.then() for one-time value handling or actions, not for assertions that need automatic retries.
gotchas: Do not use cy.then() when the callback must retry. Use .should() with a callback for retryable assertions.
Return a value or use a Cypress query instead of passing a returned DOM element into later commands.
Do not mix Cypress commands with a synchronous return value in the same callback. Cypress reports an async and sync code error.
Do not use await to control Cypress commands. Cypress places commands in its own serial queue.

cy.tick.summary: cy.tick() advances the fake clock by a chosen number of milliseconds. Use cy.clock() first so Cypress controls native time functions and runs timers scheduled in that interval.
cy.tick.explanation: Call cy.clock() first to replace the browser's native time functions. Then cy.tick(milliseconds) advances the controlled clock, and Cypress runs timers whose scheduled times fall within that interval. The command yields a clock object, which also provides tick() and restore() methods.

parameters.name: milliseconds
parameters.description: Number of milliseconds by which to advance the controlled clock.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings object. The documented option is log, which controls Command Log output and defaults to true.

cy.tick.returns: A clock object with tick(milliseconds) and restore() methods.

example.title: Trigger a timer
example.code:
cy.clock()
cy.visit('/index.html')
cy.window().invoke('addIntro')
cy.tick(500)
cy.get('#header').should('have.text', 'Hello, World')
example.explanation: The test freezes time, starts the app, advances the clock by 500 milliseconds, and checks the text set by the timer.

useCases.title: Test delayed behavior
useCases.scenario: Move past a setTimeout or other controlled timer and verify the resulting application state.

useCases.title: Test time-based states
useCases.scenario: Advance time in small steps to test several timer-driven states without waiting in real time.

useCases.title: Restore the clock
useCases.scenario: Return the application to normal native time functions before continuing a test section.

interview.question: What does cy.tick() do?
interview.answer: cy.tick() moves the fake clock forward by a chosen number of milliseconds. Timers scheduled during that affected period are executed.
interview.followUp: How do you make cy.tick() control browser time? Call cy.clock() before it so Cypress replaces the native time functions.

interview.question: What are the main requirements for cy.tick()?
interview.answer: It requires a preceding cy.clock() call and must be chained from cy. It cannot time out because it is a utility command.
interview.followUp: What happens if cy.clock() is missing? The command cannot control the native timers as required by the API.

interview.question: What does cy.tick() yield?
interview.answer: The command yields a clock object. That object has tick(milliseconds) for advancing time and restore() for returning native time functions to normal.
interview.followUp: How can the clock be restored without calling restore() in a callback? Use cy.clock().invoke('restore').

keyPoints: Pass the time increment as a number of milliseconds.
Timers scheduled inside the advanced interval run when the clock moves.
The log option controls whether the command appears in Cypress's Command Log; its default is true.
A then() callback can access the clock through this.clock.
The command has no timeout period.
gotchas: Call cy.clock() before cy.tick(); otherwise the native time functions have not been overridden.
cy.tick() does not perform assertions; later assertions continue through it normally.
The clock is restored automatically between tests, so manual restoration is usually unnecessary.

cy.title.explanation: `cy.title()` gets the title of the page currently shown in the Cypress application preview. It can be followed by a Cypress assertion, such as checking that the title includes expected text.
cy.title.returns: The current page title, which can be checked with Cypress assertions.

useCases.title: Debug a title check
useCases.scenario: Investigate a failed end-to-end test in the Cypress runner.

interview.question: What does `cy.title()` do?
interview.answer: `cy.title()` reads the title of the current page. In an end-to-end test, the page is commonly opened first with `cy.visit()`, then the title is checked with an assertion.
interview.followUp: How can you check only part of a title? Use an assertion such as `.should('include', 'Expected text')`.

interview.question: Where does `cy.title()` get the title from?
interview.answer: It is used in end-to-end testing because the test interacts with an application loaded in the Application Under Test area. The Cypress example visits a URL and then checks the page title.
interview.followUp: Where can you inspect the result while developing? Use the Test Runner, where commands appear in the Command Log and the application remains interactive.

interview.question: How is `cy.title()` normally used in a test?
interview.answer: The method returns the current page title so a following Cypress assertion can verify it. A typical check is `cy.title().should('include', 'Kitchen Sink')`.
interview.followUp: How would you debug a failed title check? Run the spec in open mode and inspect the application preview, Command Log, and browser developer tools.

keyPoints: Use `cy.title()` to read the current page title, then chain a Cypress assertion to check its value.
The title belongs to the application loaded in the end-to-end test preview.
Run the test in the Cypress Test Runner to see the command and investigate failures during local development.
The loaded page remains inspectable in browser developer tools while the test runs.

cy.trigger.summary: cy.trigger() dispatches a DOM event on an element, window, or document. Use it when an event handler needs an event that commands such as click() or type() do not fire.
cy.trigger.explanation: Use cy.trigger() to dispatch a DOM event on an element, window, or document. Cypress can calculate event coordinates from a position or explicit coordinates, and options can add event properties or change behavior such as bubbling and actionability checks.
cy.trigger.syntax:
.trigger(eventName)
.trigger(eventName, position)
.trigger(eventName, options)
.trigger(eventName, x, y)
.trigger(eventName, position, options)
.trigger(eventName, x, y, options)

parameters.name: eventName
parameters.description: The event name. It must be a non-empty string.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: A named event position. The default is center.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Horizontal pixels from the element's left edge.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Vertical pixels from the element's top edge.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options that change event creation, coordinates, actionability, and other behavior.

cy.trigger.returns: The same subject passed to cy.trigger().

example.explanation: This sends a mouseover event to the button and checks that the tooltip appears.

useCases.title: Test global keyboard shortcuts
useCases.scenario: Send a shortcut to a handler registered on the document.

interview.question: What does cy.trigger() do?
interview.answer: cy.trigger() dispatches a named DOM event on the current subject. It can target an element, window, or document, and it accepts positions, coordinates, and event options.
interview.followUp: How would you send a global keyboard shortcut? Use cy.document().trigger('keydown', { key: 'k', ctrlKey: true }).

interview.question: How does cy.trigger() handle event coordinates?
interview.answer: By default, Cypress calculates client, page, and screen coordinates from the target and the supplied position or coordinates. Values explicitly passed in options override those calculated values.
interview.followUp: Why might clientX and pageX differ? They use different origins: the viewport and the document, respectively.

interview.question: When should keyboard input use cy.press() instead of cy.trigger()?
interview.answer: The command creates one keyboard event with the properties supplied, such as key and modifier flags, but it does not move focus. For a user-like single key press, cy.press() is preferred because trigger events have isTrusted set to false.
interview.followUp: What should be used to type text? Use cy.type(), rather than constructing keyboard events with trigger().

keyPoints: It can dispatch mouse, keyboard, touch, pointer, drag-and-drop, and custom events.
You can choose a named location such as topRight or pass x and y offsets from the element's top-left corner.
Options can provide values such as clientX, shiftKey, dataTransfer, pointerId, or custom event data.
Set bubbles: false when the event must stop at the target element.
Forcing dispatches the event immediately, which is useful for hidden native controls.
Mouse-based drag handlers attached to the document can receive events triggered on the draggable element.
gotchas: The command yields the same subject, but chaining commands that depend on that subject is unsafe.
The target normally must be actionable. Use force: true for an intentionally hidden element that still needs to receive the event.
trigger() cannot activate styles that depend only on CSS :hover. Use a hover-specific workaround when needed.
The event name must contain at least one character.

cy.type.summary: Use cy.type() to enter text or keyboard sequences into a supported DOM element. It can also test shortcuts, modifiers, contenteditable fields, and some special input types.
cy.type.explanation: Cypress first gets a DOM element, then .type() sends keyboard input to it. The command can parse special sequences inside braces, such as {enter} or {selectAll}. It waits for the element to be actionable unless force is enabled.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: String to enter into the target DOM element. It may contain parsed special key sequences.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings such as delay, force, timeout, release, and special-sequence parsing.

cy.type.returns: The same subject that was passed to .type().

example.explanation: This finds a focusable input and types an email address into it.

useCases.scenario: Fill a text field, textarea, password field, or contenteditable element during an end-to-end test.

useCases.title: Test keyboard shortcuts
useCases.scenario: Send sequences such as {ctrl+s}, {enter}, or arrow keys to test keyboard behavior.

useCases.title: Control typing speed
useCases.scenario: Use delay to imitate slower human typing in an input or editable element.

useCases.title: Test document-level shortcuts
useCases.scenario: Type into body when the application listens for global keyboard events.

interview.question: How do you type text with Cypress?
interview.answer: Use cy.get() to select a supported, focusable DOM element, then call .type(text). Cypress waits for actionability and focuses the element before typing if needed.
interview.followUp: How can typing be forced? Pass { force: true }. This skips the normal actionability checks and fires the events automatically.

interview.question: How are special keys and modifiers handled?
interview.answer: Text inside braces can represent special keys, such as {enter}, {backspace}, and {selectAll}. Set parseSpecialCharSequences to false when braces must be entered literally.
interview.followUp: How would you keep a modifier active for later commands? Use {release: false}; Cypress releases modifiers between tests automatically.

interview.question: What options control typing behavior?
interview.answer: The command uses .type(text) or .type(text, options). Useful options include delay, timeout, force, parseSpecialCharSequences, release, scrollBehavior, and waitForAnimations.
interview.followUp: What happens when the subject is not focused? Cypress clicks it first, then emits keyboard events such as keydown, input, and keyup.

keyPoints: The text can include special sequences for navigation, deletion, selection, and other keyboard actions.
Typing is immediate by default. Set delay to add a pause after each keypress.
The command yields the original subject, but relying on it after typing is unsafe.
force: true bypasses actionability checks when the test must type regardless of the element state.
Typing produces keyboard and input events that match the pressed keys, including keydown, keyup, and input when applicable.
Use body for document-level keyboard shortcuts or modifier-key actions on arbitrary elements.
gotchas: Do not depend on the same subject after typing. Start a new query when the element may become stale.
Date, month, week, and time inputs use documented value formats and do not accept special character sequences.
For editable rich text, select the element with contenteditable itself, not a child node.

cy.uncheck.summary: `cy.uncheck()` clears checkbox elements yielded by a previous Cypress command. It can clear all matched checkboxes or only those with selected values.
cy.uncheck.explanation: Chain `.uncheck()` from a command that yields checkbox elements. Without an argument, it clears all matched checkboxes. A string selects one value, and an array selects several. Cypress waits until the elements can be acted on, then yields the original subject or only the matching elements.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value of the checkbox to clear.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: The values of the checkboxes to clear.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options such as `force`, `timeout`, `waitForAnimations`, `scrollBehavior`, and `log`.

cy.uncheck.returns: The same subject, or the matching checkbox elements when a value or values argument is supplied.

example.title: Uncheck selected values
example.explanation: This finds checkbox inputs and clears the ones whose values are `ga` or `ca`.

useCases.title: Reset checkbox choices
useCases.scenario: Clear every checkbox in a group before setting a known selection.

useCases.title: Uncheck one value
useCases.scenario: Clear one checkbox selected by its HTML value.

useCases.title: Uncheck multiple values
useCases.scenario: Clear several checkbox values in one command.

interview.question: How do you uncheck only selected checkbox values?
interview.answer: Call `cy.get()` to yield checkbox elements, then call `.uncheck()`. Cypress can clear every matched checkbox, or only those whose values match a string or array.
interview.followUp: What happens when a value matches no checkbox? Cypress ignores that value and does not fail the command.

interview.question: What does Cypress wait for before unchecking?
interview.answer: `.uncheck()` is an action command. Cypress waits for the element to become actionable, including the normal visibility and animation checks.
interview.followUp: How can you bypass actionability checks? Pass `{ force: true }`, which forces the action.

interview.question: What does `.uncheck()` yield?
interview.answer: The command yields the same subject when no value filter is used. With a value or array, it yields only the matching checkbox elements.
interview.followUp: Why should later subject-dependent commands be avoided? Cypress marks chaining such commands as unsafe after `.uncheck()`.

keyPoints: Use `.uncheck()` to clear one or more checkbox elements.
Pass one string to target a checkbox by its `value`.
Pass an array to target multiple checkbox values.
With no value filter, the command yields the original subject.
A value filter makes the yielded subject contain only matching elements.
Cypress waits for the checkbox to become actionable before acting.
gotchas: Do not use later commands that depend on the subject after calling `.uncheck()`.
The yielded elements must be checkboxes. Radio buttons and other elements are invalid.
A checkbox without a `value` attribute cannot be selected by passing `on`; Cypress reports an error.
An already-clear checkbox is skipped, so no click or change event occurs.

cy.url.summary: cy.url() gets the complete URL of the page under test. It yields the URL through the Cypress chain, so use assertions, .then(), or an alias to work with the string.
cy.url.explanation: cy.url() reads the complete URL of the page under test and yields it as a string through the Cypress command chain. Use a following assertion or a .then() callback to read that value; the command itself does not return a string immediately.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings: decode defaults to false, log defaults to true, and timeout defaults to defaultCommandTimeout.

cy.url.returns: The current URL as a string, corresponding to the href value.

useCases.title: Verify redirects

interview.question: What does cy.url() yield?
interview.answer: It yields the current full URL as a string through the Cypress chain. It is equivalent to cy.location('href').
interview.followUp: How would you check only the path? Use cy.location('pathname') and assert that value.

interview.question: When should you use the decode option?
interview.answer: Pass { decode: true } to decode the URL with decodeURI() before Cypress yields it. This is useful when the URL contains readable non-ASCII characters.
interview.followUp: Will every encoded character be decoded? No. Reserved characters such as ampersands and slashes remain encoded.

interview.question: How does cy.url() behave during redirects and cross-origin navigation?
interview.answer: cy.url() retries while its chained assertions are failing, so it can wait for an application redirect. It can also read the URL after navigation to another origin.
interview.followUp: Can you interact with the other origin immediately? No. Use cy.origin() for commands that interact with that page.

keyPoints: Use cy.url() to inspect the complete URL of the current page.
Use cy.location('href') when you want the same full-URL value through the location command.
The command accepts an options object for decoding, logging, and timeout settings.
Set decode: true when assertions should use readable non-ASCII URL characters.
You can safely attach assertions or other compatible commands after cy.url().
Use a regular expression with .should('match', ...) when part of the URL is generated.
gotchas: Do not assign cy.url() to a variable expecting a URL string. Use .then() or an alias instead.
The result includes the protocol, host, port, path, query string, and hash. Use cy.location() when you only need one part.
A URL assertion can wait for navigation or a redirect. You usually do not need cy.wait() before it.

interview.question: How do you set a viewport in Cypress?
interview.answer: Use cy.viewport(width, height) for exact pixel dimensions. You can also use a supported preset such as 'iphone-6'.
interview.followUp: How would you use landscape mode? Pass the preset and the string 'landscape', such as cy.viewport('iphone-6', 'landscape').

interview.question: How do presets and orientation work?
interview.answer: The command accepts a preset and an orientation. The default orientation is portrait, while landscape swaps the preset's width and height.
interview.followUp: What happens to an iPhone 6 preset in landscape mode? Its 375 by 667 dimensions become 667 by 375.

interview.question: When should you use configuration instead of cy.viewport()?
interview.answer: Set viewportWidth and viewportHeight in Cypress configuration for defaults. During a test, use cy.viewport(), because Cypress.config() cannot change those values for the current test.
interview.followUp: How can one suite use a different viewport without calling cy.viewport()? Pass viewportWidth and viewportHeight in the suite or test configuration object.

Custom width values must be finite and at least zero.
Custom height values must be finite and at least zero.
If you provide a preset without an orientation, Cypress uses portrait mode.
Cypress keeps the viewport dimensions associated with each command snapshot.
The viewport returns to its configured default between tests.

Changing the viewport does not simulate the device pixel ratio.
Do not change viewportWidth or viewportHeight with Cypress.config() while a test runs. Use cy.viewport() or test configuration instead.

interview.question: What does cy.visit() wait for?
interview.answer: cy.visit() loads a URL and waits for the page's load event before resolving. It yields the page window object.
interview.followUp: What should be registered before visiting an app that sends startup requests? Register cy.intercept() first, because an intercept added after cy.visit() may miss those requests.

interview.question: How does cy.visit() handle relative URLs?
interview.answer: With baseUrl configured, Cypress prefixes a relative URL with that value. Without baseUrl, a fully qualified URL is needed, or Cypress can serve a local file.
interview.followUp: How do you visit another host when baseUrl is configured? Pass the full URL to cy.visit().

interview.question: How do you test a 404 page with cy.visit()?
interview.answer: By default, visits fail for response codes outside the 2xx and 3xx ranges. Set failOnStatusCode to false when testing an error page.
interview.followUp: How can a visit tolerate a temporary server error? Set retryOnStatusCodeFailure to true; Cypress retries up to four times.

keyPoints: The command resolves after the page load event and yields the remote page window.
A configured baseUrl is added to relative visit paths.
Use qs to add query parameters without building the query string yourself.
Use onBeforeLoad to prepare browser state before application scripts run.
Use onLoad for code that needs page resources to be available.
gotchas: Do not rely on the yielded window for later commands. Use .then() when you need direct access to it.
Custom headers apply only to the first page request, not to requests started by the page.
Use cy.origin() to interact with a different origin in the same test. Cross-origin visits do not support onBeforeLoad or onLoad.

cy.wait.summary: Use cy.wait() to pause for a fixed time or wait for an intercepted request. Alias waits yield request and response data and can wait for one or more aliases.
cy.wait.explanation: cy.wait() pauses the command queue until a time passes or an aliased request finishes. With an alias, Cypress first waits for the request to start and then for its response. It yields the request and response details, so later commands can check them.

cy.wait(time)
cy.wait(alias)
cy.wait(aliases)
cy.wait(time, options)
cy.wait(alias, options)

parameters.description: Milliseconds to wait.

parameters.name: alias

parameters.name: aliases

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options such as log, timeout, requestTimeout, and responseTimeout.

cy.wait.returns: With a time argument, cy.wait() yields the same subject it received. With an alias, it yields an interception object containing the HTTP request and response properties. With aliases, it yields an array of interceptions.

example.explanation: This watches the account request and checks its response status.

useCases.title: Inspect network traffic

useCases.title: Coordinate multiple requests
useCases.scenario: Wait for several dashboard requests together.

useCases.title: Add a fixed delay
useCases.scenario: Use a controlled delay when a time-based test is specifically required.

interview.question: What does cy.wait() support?
interview.answer: Use cy.wait(milliseconds) for a delay, or cy.wait('@alias') after assigning an intercepted route an alias. An alias wait waits for the matching request and its response, then yields an interception object.
interview.followUp: How do you wait for several requests? Pass an array such as cy.wait(['@users', '@activities']); Cypress waits for all of them and yields an array in the same alias order.

interview.question: How are aliased waits timed out?
interview.answer: An aliased wait has two phases. requestTimeout controls how long Cypress waits for the matching request to start, and responseTimeout controls how long it waits for the server response.
interview.followUp: Which defaults apply? The documented defaults are 5000 ms for requestTimeout and 30000 ms for responseTimeout.

interview.question: Do assertions after cy.wait() retry?
interview.answer: A direct assertion after cy.wait() gets one attempt because cy.wait() is not a query. Adding .its() or .invoke() starts a retryable query chain, so the following assertion can retry until its timeout.
interview.followUp: How can that query fail immediately? Set the query timeout to 0, for example .its('response.statusCode', { timeout: 0 }).

keyPoints: A numeric argument makes Cypress wait for that many milliseconds.
A string argument names a route alias created with as(), and the name is referenced with @.
An alias array waits for every listed request before the command resolves.
A single alias yields an interception with request and response information.
Repeated waits for the same alias move through matching responses in order.
JSON response bodies become objects only when the response declares the JSON content type; otherwise the body can be a string.
The options object can override the request and response timeout settings for the wait.
gotchas: Avoid fixed time waits when a request alias or assertion can express the condition.
A direct assertion checks the yielded interception once. Use a query such as its() before the assertion when retrying is needed.
An alias wait can fail before a response phase if no matching request starts within requestTimeout.
After a millisecond wait, do not rely on the yielded subject for later commands.

cy.window.summary: Gets the window object for the active application under test. You can chain commands and assertions to inspect it or wait for application state.
cy.window.explanation: `cy.window()` gets the window object belonging to the active application under test. It is a query, so Cypress can retry it while chained assertions run, and later commands can use the yielded object.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: An optional object with `log` and `timeout` settings.

cy.window.returns: The window object of the application under test, typed as an AUTWindow object in TypeScript.

example.title: Wait for app readiness and check a window property
example.explanation: This waits for the app to report that it is ready, then checks a custom window value.

useCases.title: Wait for the application to be ready
useCases.scenario: Read application state stored on `window`, such as a custom readiness flag.

useCases.title: Check custom window properties
useCases.scenario: Inspect custom fields attached to the application window.

useCases.title: Compare event types across window realms
useCases.scenario: Use the application's browser constructors when testing events.

interview.question: What does `cy.window()` yield?
interview.answer: It yields the active application's window object. Because it is a query, chained commands and assertions can use that object.
interview.followUp: How can a test wait for an application readiness flag? Use `cy.window().should('have.property', 'appReady', true)` after visiting the page.

interview.question: Which options does `cy.window()` accept?
interview.answer: Pass an options object, such as `{ timeout: 10000 }`. The `log` option controls Command Log output, and `timeout` controls how long Cypress waits.
interview.followUp: What does the timeout affect when an assertion is chained? The timeout is passed through to the chained `.should()` assertion.

interview.question: How should tests access custom window properties?
interview.answer: Use `cy.window().then((win) => { ... })` when code must access the yielded window. For custom TypeScript properties, augment `Cypress.ApplicationWindow` so the property is typed.
interview.followUp: Why might `event instanceof KeyboardEvent` fail? Cypress and the application use different window realms, so compare with `event instanceof win.KeyboardEvent`.

keyPoints: The command returns the active page's application window.
Use the yielded value in `.then()`, or continue with commands such as `.its()` and `.should()`.
Chaining is supported, and assertions can cause Cypress to retry the query.
The options are `log`, which defaults to true, and `timeout`, which defaults to `defaultCommandTimeout`.
A chained assertion can make Cypress wait until the required window state exists.
Add application-specific window fields to this interface to prevent TypeScript errors.
gotchas: Do not read a value in ordinary code immediately after `cy.window()`. Put dependent checks inside a `.then()` callback or a later Cypress command.
Browser classes can come from different window objects. For event checks, use the class from the yielded application window, such as `win.KeyboardEvent`.
Start the command with `cy.window()`; it cannot be called as a standalone function.

cy.within.summary: `cy.within()` scopes Cypress commands to one DOM element, such as a form or table row. It keeps the original element as its yielded subject.
cy.within.explanation: Chain `within()` from a command that yields one DOM element. Cypress then runs commands inside the callback against that element. The callback receives the element as its first argument. The command itself still yields the original element, not anything returned inside the callback.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: Function called with the current yielded subject as its first argument.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings object. The documented option is `log`, which defaults to `true` and controls Command Log output.

cy.within.returns: The same subject passed into `within()`. It is unsafe to chain later commands that depend on this subject.

example.explanation: The inner queries search only inside the form. `cy.root()` gets that scoped form so the test can submit it.

useCases.title: Test fields inside a form

useCases.title: Work with one table row
useCases.scenario: A table contains repeated rows, and the test must inspect or click cells in the row containing known text.

useCases.title: Act on the scoped element
useCases.scenario: A scoped form needs an action on the form itself, such as submit.

interview.question: What does `cy.within()` do?
interview.answer: `within()` scopes later Cypress commands to one yielded DOM element. For example, after `cy.get('form').within(...)`, inner `cy.get()` calls search inside that form instead of the whole document.
interview.followUp: How do you leave the scope temporarily? Start a new chain with `cy.root()` and use `.closest()` to move to an ancestor outside the scoped element.

interview.question: What are the subject and chaining rules for `within()`?
interview.answer: It requires a previous command that yields exactly one DOM element or the document. It yields the same subject it received, so it does not yield an element found inside its callback.
interview.followUp: What should you use when the inner element must become the subject? Query it directly with `.find()` or another command after selecting the parent.

interview.question: How can a test submit or otherwise act on the scoped element?
interview.answer: Commands inside the callback are automatically rooted at the scoped element. `cy.root()` inside the callback returns that scoped element, which is useful for actions such as submitting a form.
interview.followUp: Does `within()` wait for or retry assertions? No. Assertions chained to `within()` run once, and the command cannot time out.

keyPoints: It limits commands in the callback to the selected element's contents.
The callback receives the current subject as its first parameter.
The command keeps the original parent element as its yielded subject.
Inside the callback, `cy.get()` searches within the scope rather than across the complete document.
Use `cy.root()` to access the element that defines the current scope.
Since version 12.0.0, multiple yielded elements cause an error.
gotchas: Do not chain subject-dependent commands after `within()` because the yielded subject may not be safe to use.
The previous command must yield exactly one DOM element or the document. A selector matching several elements is invalid.
Returning another element, or using `cy.wrap()` inside the callback, does not change what `within()` yields.
Assertions chained to `within()` run once; `within()` itself does not retry them.

cy.wrap.summary: `cy.wrap()` yields an object, element, or promise value as a Cypress subject. For promises, it waits for resolution before continuing.
cy.wrap.explanation: `cy.wrap()` turns an object, element, or promise into the current Cypress subject. Cypress waits for a wrapped promise to resolve, then passes its value to the next command or assertion. Use `.then()` when a function must not run until earlier Cypress commands finish.

parameters.name: subject
parameters.description: The object, element, or promise to yield.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options that change command behavior. `log` defaults to `true`; `timeout` defaults to `defaultCommandTimeout`.

cy.wrap.returns: Yields the supplied object, or the resolved value when the subject is a promise.

example.explanation: This waits for the promise, then checks a property of its resolved object.

useCases.title: Continue with an element

useCases.title: Re-wrap iframe content
useCases.scenario: A same-origin iframe body is a raw DOM element.

interview.question: What does `cy.wrap()` do?
interview.answer: `cy.wrap(subject)` yields the subject so Cypress commands can continue from it. If the subject is a promise, Cypress waits for resolution and yields the resolved value.
interview.followUp: Does it delay a function call that returns a promise? No. The function runs before `cy.wrap()` receives the promise, so use `.then()` to control when the function starts.

interview.question: When would you wrap an object or element?
interview.answer: Use it to continue Cypress commands from a raw object or element, such as invoking an object method or clicking a conditionally selected element. It also lets assertions run against a resolved promise value.
interview.followUp: Why wrap a raw iframe body? Wrapping restores a Cypress subject so later queries, actions, and assertions can use Cypress retry behavior.

interview.question: Which options does `cy.wrap()` accept?
interview.answer: The `timeout` option controls how long Cypress waits for `cy.wrap()` to resolve. `log` controls whether the command appears in the Command Log.
interview.followUp: Can wrapping time out because of assertions? Yes. `cy.wrap()` can time out while chained assertions are still failing.

keyPoints: It yields the value supplied to the command.
For promises, the yielded subject is the resolved value.
A wrapped promise is awaited before the next command or assertion runs.
Wrapping a jQuery element lets you continue with Cypress commands such as `.click()`.
Chained assertions can cause the command to retry until they pass.
Since version 3.2.0, an undefined subject is retried when followed by `.should()`.
gotchas: Wrapping a promise does not delay the function call that created it. Start dependent work inside `.then()` after earlier Cypress commands complete.
A rejected wrapped promise fails the test.
Call it as `cy.wrap(...)`; it is not a standalone command.

cy.writeFile.summary: cy.writeFile() writes text or structured data to a file under the Cypress project root. It creates missing paths, overwrites files by default, and can use encodings or file options.
cy.writeFile.explanation: Call cy.writeFile() with a path and data. Cypress writes the data under the project root, creates missing folders, and replaces an existing file by default. You can set an encoding or options such as append mode. The command yields null after the write succeeds.

cy.writeFile(filePath, contents)
cy.writeFile(filePath, contents, encoding)
cy.writeFile(filePath, contents, options)

interview.question: What does cy.writeFile() do?
interview.answer: It writes String, Array, Object, or Buffer data to a file path relative to the project root. Missing folders are created, and an existing file is replaced unless the file-system flag changes that behavior.
interview.followUp: How would you append data? Use an options object such as { flag: 'a+' }. For JSON, read and modify the value first, then write the complete merged value.

interview.question: How do encoding and Buffer values work?
interview.answer: The command supports encodings such as utf8, ascii, base64, hex, binary, latin1, and utf16le. Passing null as the encoding writes a Buffer directly without converting it to a string.
interview.followUp: How can encoding be combined with other options? Put encoding inside the options object, for example { encoding: 'ascii', flag: 'a+' }.

interview.question: What does cy.writeFile() yield, and when can it time out?
interview.answer: The command yields null after the file is written. It can time out when encoding takes a long time, and its timeout can be set with the timeout option.
interview.followUp: What happens if the target is inside the fixtures folder? Cypress clears that fixture's cache, so a later cy.fixture() call reads the new contents.

keyPoints: filePath is relative to the project root, which contains the Cypress configuration file.
Cypress creates both the file and missing parent folders.
The contents can be a string, array, object, or Buffer.
You can choose a supported text encoding, including ascii, base64, binary, or hex.
Use a null encoding to write a Buffer without string encoding.
The options object can control logging, file flags, encoding, and timeout.
gotchas: The default write replaces an existing file. Use an append flag when adding plain text.
Appending JSON does not merge objects. Read the object or array, change it, and write the complete value again.
Assertions after this command run only one time. They are not retried.
The command fails when Cypress cannot write to disk, including because of operating-system permissions.

interview.question: How do you create a custom Cypress command?
interview.answer: Use Cypress.Commands.add() to register a reusable command. Use Cypress.Commands.addAll() to register several commands from an object.
interview.followUp: How can a command accept the previous subject? Pass an options object with prevSubject set to true or to a subject type such as element.

interview.question: What are parent and child commands?
interview.answer: A parent command ignores an earlier subject and starts a new chain. A child command receives the earlier subject through its first callback argument.
interview.followUp: What is a dual command? Set prevSubject to optional so it can start a chain or use an existing subject.

interview.question: How do you validate a child command's subject?
interview.answer: Set prevSubject to element to require a DOM element as the previous subject. The callback receives that subject before the command's other arguments.
interview.followUp: What should the callback return when the subject must continue unchanged? Return the received subject.

Use overwrite when you need to change an existing Cypress command.
Parent commands start a new chain and do not use a previous subject.
Child commands receive the previous subject automatically in their callback.
Set prevSubject to optional for a command that supports both starting and continuing a chain.
Subject validation can require an element, document, or window.

Use a custom query when retry behavior is needed, especially when returning a DOM element.

Cypress.Commands.add.explanation: Cypress custom commands let you add commands or replace existing ones. Use add for new commands and overwrite for built-in commands. A command can start a chain, use the previous subject, or optionally support either form. Use a custom query instead when synchronous retryable behavior is needed.
